title: Skeletons and muscles: what bones do, and how muscles move them

summary.text: The muscle that bends your elbow is joined to your forearm only about 4 centimetres from the elbow. A string tied that close to a hinge has to be pulled very hard. So when you lift a 1 kilogram bag of rice, that muscle pulls with about 8 kilograms of force. Your child tests this with a ruler, a rubber band and five coins. They also name the main bones and find out what bone is made of. Then they compare our inside skeleton with the outside skeleton of a crab or an ant.
summary.art: A girl holding a cloth bag of rice with her elbow bent, and a see-through view of her arm showing the upper arm bone, the two forearm bones and one muscle joined to the forearm close to the elbow.

intro.hook: Bend your elbow and hold a 1 kilogram bag of rice in your hand. How hard is the muscle in your upper arm pulling: with 1 kilogram of force, with less, or with more?
intro.text: Most people guess 1 kilogram. The real answer is about 8 kilograms. The reason is the place where the muscle is joined to the bone. In this unit you build a ruler arm and measure what changes when the muscle is tied in different places. You name twelve bones on a real body. You freeze two slabs of ice to find out why a bone does not shatter like chalk. You also meet animals who wear their skeleton on the outside, and animals who have no hard skeleton at all.
intro.art: A wooden ruler lying on a table as a model forearm, with a finger pressing one end, a stack of coins taped to the other end, and a rubber band lifting the ruler near the pressed end.

outcomes: I can find and name twelve main bones on a body, from the skull to the shin bone.
I can explain the jobs of a skeleton: to hold the body up, to protect soft organs, to help it move, and to make blood.
I can explain that bone is alive, what it is made of, and how it grows and changes with use.
I can explain that a muscle moves a bone by contracting, and why muscles work in pairs.
I can test fairly how the place where a muscle is tied changes its force and its movement.
I can explain why muscles pull much harder than the weights we lift, using the idea of a lever.
I can compare a skeleton inside the body, a skeleton outside it and a body with none.
I can explain what the same arm bones in a human, a bat and a whale tell us.

terms.meaning: The frame of hard parts that holds up an animal's body. It also protects the soft parts and gives the muscles something to pull on.
terms.example: Your skeleton is made of 206 bones. A crab's skeleton is the hard shell on the outside of her body.
terms.art: A child standing next to a drawing of her own skeleton, the same height.

terms.meaning: The bones of the head. They make a hard box around the brain and hold the eyes, nose and teeth.
terms.example: Knock gently on the top of your head. The hard thing you feel is your skull.
terms.art: A side view of a human skull with the brain drawn faintly inside it.

terms.meaning: The chain of small bones down the middle of the back. Each small bone is called a vertebra. The backbone is also called the spine.
terms.example: Bend forward and run a finger down the middle of your back. The row of bumps is your backbone.
terms.art: A side view of a human backbone, a gentle S-shaped chain of small bones from the skull to the hips.

terms.meaning: The cage made by the ribs, the backbone and the breastbone. It protects the heart and the lungs.
terms.example: Press your fingers on your side and take a deep breath. You can feel your ribs move out.
terms.art: A rib cage seen from the front, with the heart and lungs drawn faintly inside.

terms.meaning: The ring of hip bones at the bottom of the backbone. It carries the weight of the upper body, and the thigh bones join it.
terms.example: Put your hands on your hips. The hard edges under your hands are the top of your pelvis.
terms.art: A pelvis seen from the front, a bowl-shaped ring of bone with the two thigh bones fitting into its sides.

terms.meaning: The thigh bone. It runs from the hip to the knee, and it is the longest bone in the body.
terms.example: A grown-up's femur is about a quarter of their height.
terms.art: A leg skeleton with the long thigh bone coloured, from the hip to the knee.

terms.meaning: The soft, living material inside many bones. Red marrow makes new blood cells.
terms.example: The marrow inside your hip bones and backbone is making new blood cells right now.
terms.art: A long bone cut open along its length, showing the hard wall and the soft red marrow inside.

terms.meaning: A tough, bendy protein that makes long fibres. Bone is made of collagen fibres with hard mineral packed between them.
terms.example: Collagen stops a bone from snapping like a stick of chalk.
terms.art: A zoomed-in picture of bone showing rope-like fibres with small hard crystals packed along them.

terms.meaning: A body part that can get shorter and pull. Muscles joined to bones move the skeleton.
terms.example: The biceps is the muscle at the front of your upper arm. It bends your elbow.
terms.art: An arm with the skin drawn see-through, showing the red muscle at the front of the upper arm.

terms.meaning: A muscle contracts when it gets shorter and pulls. It relaxes when it stops pulling and can be stretched long again.
terms.example: When you bend your elbow, your biceps contracts and the muscle at the back of your arm relaxes.
terms.art: Two drawings of the same arm: bent with the front muscle short and fat, and straight with the front muscle long and thin.

terms.meaning: A strong cord that joins a muscle to a bone.
terms.example: Bend your elbow and press into the bend. The tight cord you feel is the tendon of your biceps.
terms.art: A close view of a bent elbow with a white cord running from the muscle to the forearm bone.

terms.meaning: A place where two bones meet. At most joints the bones can move.
terms.example: Your elbow is a joint between the upper arm bone and the two forearm bones.
terms.art: An elbow joint with the three bones that meet there, and a curved arrow showing the bend.

terms.meaning: A stiff bar that turns about one fixed point. A push or pull at one place on the bar moves a load at another place.
terms.example: Your forearm is a lever. It turns at the elbow, the muscle pulls near the elbow, and the load is in your hand.
terms.art: A ruler turning about one end, with an arrow pulling up near that end and a weight at the far end.

terms.meaning: A skeleton inside the body, with the muscles and skin around it.
terms.example: Humans, crows, frogs, fish and lizards have an endoskeleton.
terms.art: A see-through outline of a crow with the bird's skeleton inside.

terms.meaning: A hard skeleton on the outside of the body, with the muscles inside it.
terms.example: A cockroach, a crab and a spider each have an exoskeleton.
terms.art: A crab seen from above, with the hard shell and jointed legs clearly drawn.

terms.meaning: To shed an old exoskeleton and grow a bigger one. An animal with an exoskeleton must moult to grow.
terms.example: A young cockroach moults several times before she is fully grown.
terms.art: A pale, soft cockroach climbing out of a split brown shell of her own shape.

explanations.concept: The main bones and their names
explanations.definition: A skeleton is the frame of hard parts that holds up a body. A grown-up human skeleton is usually counted as 206 bones.
explanations.description: Start at the top. The skull is a box of bones around the brain. The lower jaw is the only part of the skull that moves. The backbone is a chain of small bones called vertebrae. It runs from the skull to the hips. Twelve pairs of ribs curve round from the backbone, and most of them join the breastbone at the front. The collarbone and the shoulder blade hold each arm on. The upper arm has one bone, called the humerus. The forearm has two, called the radius and the ulna. The hip bones make a ring called the pelvis. The thigh bone is called the femur, and it is the longest bone you have. The kneecap sits in front of the knee. The lower leg has two bones. The thick one at the front is the shin bone, called the tibia. More than half of your 206 bones are in your hands and feet. A baby has more separate bones than a grown-up, because some bones join together as a child grows.
examples: Each hand has 27 bones, and each foot has 26.
The smallest bone is deep inside your ear. It is smaller than a grain of rice.
Sushruta, a surgeon of ancient India, counted 300 bones. His list included teeth and pieces of cartilage, which doctors today do not count as bones.
explanations.art: A front view of a human skeleton with twelve labels: skull, lower jaw, collarbone, shoulder blade, breastbone, ribs, backbone, humerus, radius and ulna, pelvis, femur, tibia.

explanations.definition: A skeleton holds the body up, protects soft organs and gives the muscles something to pull on. In humans and other animals with bones, it also makes blood and stores minerals.
explanations.description: The first job is support. Your body is mostly soft and wet. Without a stiff frame, a body your size would sag on the ground. The backbone and the leg bones carry your weight. The second job is protection. The skull guards the brain. The rib cage guards the heart and the lungs. The backbone guards the spinal cord, the thick bundle of nerves that runs inside it. The pelvis guards the bladder and the lower gut. The third job is movement. Bones are stiff, so a muscle that pulls on a bone moves a whole arm or leg. The fourth job is hidden. The red marrow inside your bones makes new blood cells, about two million every second. The fifth job is storage. Almost all the calcium in your body is in your bones and teeth. When your blood needs calcium, bone gives some up. Your skeleton also grows with you, so it never has to be thrown away.
examples: Support: the femur and the tibia carry your whole weight when you stand on one leg.
Protection: a cricket ball that hits a batter's chest meets the ribs first.
Movement: you can throw a ball because stiff arm bones turn at the shoulder and elbow.
explanations.art: Three small pictures in a row: a child standing straight, a rib cage around a heart and lungs, and an arm throwing a ball.

explanations.concept: Bone is alive, and it is made of two materials
explanations.definition: Bone is a living tissue. It is made of tough collagen fibres with hard mineral crystals packed between them.
explanations.description: A bone in a museum is dry and white, so people often think of bone as a kind of stone. A bone in a living body is pink, wet and full of cells. Blood vessels run through it, and nerves reach it, which is why a broken bone hurts. The hard part of bone is a mix of two materials. One is a mineral made of calcium and phosphate. The mineral is hard, but alone it would snap like chalk. The other is collagen, a protein that makes long, bendy fibres. Collagen alone would bend like rubber. Together they make a material that is both hard and tough. Most long bones are also hollow tubes with marrow inside. A tube is nearly as hard to bend as a solid rod, and it weighs much less. Bone cells never stop working. Some cells dissolve old bone, and others lay down new bone. In a grown-up, about one tenth of the skeleton is replaced each year.
examples: A chicken bone left in vinegar for some days loses its mineral and bends like rubber.
A bone that has been burnt loses its collagen and crumbles when pressed.
A broken arm in a plaster cast mends because bone cells build new bone across the break.
explanations.art: A long bone cut open to show the hard outer wall, the spongy bone at the ends and the marrow in the middle, with a small circle zooming in on fibres and crystals.

explanations.concept: How bones grow, and how they change with use
explanations.definition: A child's long bones grow at growth plates, which are bands of cartilage near each end. Bone also gets thicker where it is loaded often, and thinner where it is not.
explanations.description: Cartilage is a firm, bendy material, like the stiff part of your ear. Near each end of a child's long bone is a thin band of cartilage called a growth plate. The cartilage cells there keep dividing, and bone replaces them from behind. That makes the bone longer. By the late teens the growth plates turn into bone, and growing taller stops. Bone goes on changing all through life. Bone cells sense each load on the bone. Where a bone is bent and squeezed often, they build more bone. Where a bone is hardly used, they take bone away. The arm that a tennis player serves with has thicker bones than her other arm. Astronauts float in space and their legs carry no weight. They lose about one hundredth of the bone in their hips each month. So they exercise on machines for about two hours a day. Running, jumping and skipping in childhood build bone that lasts into old age.
examples: A doctor can tell a child's age roughly from an X-ray of the growth plates in the hand.
An arm that spends six weeks in a plaster cast comes out thinner, and its bone is lighter.
Mae Jemison, a doctor and astronaut, worked on a study of bone cells in space on her flight in 1992.
explanations.art: A child's thigh bone with a thin coloured band near each end marked as the growth plate, and small arrows showing the bone growing longer there.

explanations.concept: Muscles pull, and they never push
explanations.definition: A muscle moves a bone by contracting, which means getting shorter and pulling. A muscle cannot push. So muscles work in pairs, with one to pull each way.
explanations.description: You have more than 600 muscles joined to your skeleton. Each one is joined to bones by tendons, which are strong cords. When a muscle contracts, it pulls its two ends towards each other, and the bone on one side moves. To move the bone back, a second muscle on the other side has to pull. The biceps at the front of your upper arm bends your elbow. The triceps at the back straightens it. While one contracts, the other relaxes and is stretched long. Nearly every joint has pairs like this. Muscles also work when nothing moves. When you stand still, muscles in your legs, back and neck pull gently all the time. They stop your skeleton folding at the joints. That pulling uses energy from your food and makes heat. This is one reason you feel warm after running.
examples: Bend your knee: the muscles at the back of your thigh contract. Straighten it: the muscles at the front contract.
Rise on your toes: your calf muscle contracts and pulls your heel up.
Shivering is many muscles contracting quickly, and the heat warms you.
explanations.art: An arm shown twice: bent, with the front muscle short and an arrow pulling up, and straight, with the back muscle short and an arrow pulling the other way.

explanations.concept: What happens inside a muscle when it contracts
explanations.definition: A muscle is made of long cells called muscle fibres. Inside each fibre are two kinds of very thin threads that slide past each other. When they slide together, the fibre gets shorter.
explanations.description: A muscle fibre is thinner than a hair and can be several centimetres long. Under a strong microscope, a fibre shows thousands of tiny stripes. In 1954 two pairs of scientists worked out what the stripes mean. Jean Hanson and Hugh Huxley worked in the United States. Andrew Huxley and Rolf Niedergerke worked in England. Both pairs found that a muscle has thick threads and thin threads lying side by side. When the muscle contracts, the threads do not shrink. Later work showed how they move. When a nerve sends a signal, tiny hooks on the thick threads catch the thin threads and pull them along. The threads slide over each other, like the fingers of your two hands sliding together. Each tiny pull uses energy that the cell gets from food. Millions of threads sliding a tiny distance add up to a muscle that shortens by a few centimetres.
examples: Lace the fingers of your two hands loosely and slide them together. Your hands get closer, but no finger gets shorter.
A muscle that is used hard grows more threads inside each fibre, so the muscle gets thicker.
The meat of a chicken leg pulls apart into strings. Each string is a bundle of muscle fibres.
explanations.art: Two rows of thick and thin threads, first only partly overlapping and then slid far together, with the whole length shorter in the second row.

explanations.concept: Bones are levers, and muscles pull close to the joint
explanations.definition: A lever is a stiff bar that turns about one fixed point. A forearm is a lever that turns at the elbow. The muscle pulls close to the elbow, and the load is far away in the hand.
explanations.description: A door is a lever that turns at its hinges. Push a door near the handle and it opens easily. Push it near the hinges and you must push much harder, though your hand moves only a little way. Your biceps is like the push near the hinges. Its tendon joins the forearm about 4 centimetres from the elbow in a grown-up. The middle of the hand is about 32 centimetres from the elbow. That is 8 times as far. So to hold a load in the hand, the muscle must pull about 8 times as hard as the load. This looks like a bad bargain, but the body gains two things. When the muscle shortens by 1 centimetre, the hand moves about 8 centimetres. The hand also moves 8 times as fast as the muscle shortens. Muscles are strong but can shorten only a little. The skeleton turns a short, strong pull into a long, quick movement. That is how you can throw a ball or swat a mosquito.
examples: In the Ruler Arm experiment, the rubber band tied nearest the pressed end stretches most and is lifted the least.
Your calf muscle pulls on the heel bone, close to the ankle, and lifts your whole body onto your toes.
A jaw closes hardest at the back teeth, which are nearest the jaw joint. That is why you crack a nut at the back of your mouth.
explanations.art: A side view of a bent arm holding a bag, with a short arrow at the muscle's tendon near the elbow and a long line from the elbow to the hand, marked 4 centimetres and 32 centimetres.

explanations.concept: Three kinds of skeleton: inside, outside and none that is hard
explanations.definition: An endoskeleton is a skeleton inside the body. An exoskeleton is a hard skeleton on the outside. Some animals have no hard skeleton, and their bodies are held firm by liquid under pressure.
explanations.description: Animals with a backbone are called vertebrates. Fish, frogs, lizards, birds and mammals, including us, are vertebrates. All have an endoskeleton, with the muscles wrapped round the bones. Animals without a backbone are called invertebrates, and they have many body plans. Insects, spiders, crabs, prawns and centipedes have an exoskeleton. It is a hard coat made mostly of a tough material called chitin. Their muscles are inside the coat and pull on it from within. The coat has thin, bendy places at the joints, so the legs can fold. A snail's shell is also a hard outside part, and the snail adds to the rim while growing. Earthworms, jellyfish and slugs have no hard skeleton. An earthworm's body is a row of rings filled with liquid, and their muscles squeeze against that liquid. The octopus has no hard skeleton either. Her only hard part is a beak.
examples: Endoskeleton: a crow, a rohu fish, a house gecko, an elephant, a human.
Exoskeleton: an ant, a cockroach, a prawn, a scorpion, a crab.
No hard skeleton: an earthworm, a jellyfish, a slug, an octopus.
explanations.art: Three animals side by side, each cut through to show the plan: a fish with bones inside, a crab with a hard coat outside and muscles within, and an earthworm with liquid-filled rings.

explanations.concept: Each kind of skeleton has gains and costs
explanations.definition: No kind of skeleton is the best. Each one solves some problems and causes others.
explanations.description: An exoskeleton is armour and frame in one. It keeps water in, which helps a small animal on dry land. But a hard coat cannot stretch. To grow, the animal must moult. She splits the old coat, climbs out, and swells before the new coat hardens. For hours or days she is soft and easy to catch. A thick coat is also heavy for a large body, so animals with an exoskeleton are mostly small. The largest on land is the coconut crab, who lives on islands such as the Nicobars. She can weigh about 4 kilograms. An endoskeleton grows along with the body, so it is never shed. It can hold up a huge body, such as an elephant or a blue whale. But it leaves the soft outside of the body open to bites, cuts and drying. A body with no hard skeleton can squeeze through tiny gaps and needs no moult. But without stiff levers, moving on land is slow and takes a lot of muscle. Counted by the number of kinds, animals with an exoskeleton are far ahead. More than three out of every four known kinds of animal are insects, spiders, crabs and their relatives.
examples: A cockroach who has just moulted is white and soft for a few hours.
A blue whale is about 30 metres long, and water helps to carry the weight of her bones.
An octopus can pass through any hole that is bigger than her beak.
explanations.art: A table with three rows for inside skeleton, outside skeleton and no hard skeleton, and columns headed Grows with the body, Protects the outside, Can be very large and Can squeeze through gaps, filled with ticks and crosses.

explanations.concept: Tricky cases: a tortoise, a shark and a starfish
explanations.definition: The place of the hard part, inside or outside, does not always tell you the kind of skeleton. You have to ask what the hard part is made from and whether it is under the skin.
explanations.description: A tortoise looks like an animal with an exoskeleton. But the shell is part of the endoskeleton. It is made from the ribs and the backbone, grown wide and joined together. A layer of horny plates covers it. A tortoise cannot leave the shell, just as you cannot leave your rib cage. A shark has an endoskeleton with no bone in it. The whole skeleton is cartilage, the same bendy material as your ear. Your own skeleton began as cartilage before you were born, and most of it turned to bone later. A starfish feels hard and looks armoured. But the hard parts are thousands of tiny plates that lie under the skin. So a starfish has an endoskeleton too, though starfish are invertebrates.
examples: A tortoise's shell has nerves and blood in it, and she can feel a touch on it.
The tip of your nose and the rim of your ear are cartilage, with no bone inside.
A dried starfish on a beach is stiff because of the small plates under the skin.
explanations.art: A tortoise skeleton seen from below, showing the backbone and ribs spreading out to form the inside of the shell.

explanations.concept: The same bones in an arm, a wing and a flipper
explanations.definition: The front limbs of all four-limbed vertebrates are built from the same set of bones, in the same order. Scientists call parts like these homologous, which means they come from the same part in a shared ancestor.
explanations.description: Your arm has one bone above the elbow and two below it. Then come the small wrist bones and five sets of finger bones. A bat's wing has the same bones. Her finger bones are very long and thin, and skin is stretched between them. A whale's flipper has them too, short and flat, packed inside a paddle. So do a crow's wing, a frog's front leg and a cat's front leg. The jobs are very different: holding, flying, swimming, hopping and running. An engineer who started fresh would not build a wing and a flipper from the same parts. The English scientist Richard Owen described this pattern carefully in the 1840s. In 1859 Charles Darwin gave the reason that scientists accept today. All these animals come from the same ancestors, who had a limb with these bones. Over millions of years the same bones changed shape for different jobs.
examples: The long thin bones in a bat's wing are the bones of her fingers.
A whale's flipper holds an upper arm bone, two forearm bones, wrist bones and finger bones.
A giraffe and a mouse each have seven bones in the neck, as you do.
explanations.art: Four front limbs drawn side by side with matching bones in matching colours: a human arm, a bat's wing, a whale's flipper and a crow's wing.

explanations.concept: Why did animals first make bone?
explanations.definition: The first animals with bone lived in the sea more than 450 million years ago. Their bone was not inside them. It was a coat of bony plates in the skin. Scientists do not agree on why bone first appeared.
explanations.description: Fossils show that bone began on the outside of early fish, as armour plates. No animal had a bony backbone until much later. Scientists have offered several reasons, and each fits some of the evidence.
examples: The oldest fossil fish with bone have a bony head shield and no bony backbone.
The flat bones on top of your skull form in a sheet of soft tissue, with no cartilage stage. The first armour formed that way too.

perspectives.who: The armour idea, put forward by the American fossil scientist Alfred Romer in 1933
perspectives.explanation: Large sea scorpions hunted in the same waters. Bony plates protected the early fish from them. Bone began as a shield.
Animals need calcium and phosphate every minute for their nerves and muscles. Plates of bone in the skin were a store. The body could draw on it when the water had too little. Bone began as a larder.
The first bony plates lay around organs that sense tiny electric signals in the water. Hard mineral may have shielded those organs and helped them work. Bone began as part of a sense.

explanations.art: An early jawless fish with a wide bony head shield and a soft tail, swimming near the sea floor while a large sea scorpion approaches.

agreed.text: Bone is a living tissue that is taken apart and rebuilt all through life.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, bone is full of living cells and blood vessels. Broken bones heal, and X-rays show bone getting thicker or thinner over months.

agreed.text: Bone is made of collagen fibres and a hard mineral of calcium and phosphate.
agreed.evidence: Acid dissolves the mineral and leaves a bendy bone made of collagen. Burning removes the collagen and leaves a brittle bone made of mineral.

agreed.text: Muscles can only pull, and they shorten because thin threads inside them slide past each other.
agreed.evidence: In 1954 Jean Hanson and Hugh Huxley studied muscle fibres under microscopes. So did Andrew Huxley and Rolf Niedergerke. Both pairs saw the bands in a fibre move closer while the threads stayed the same length.

agreed.text: Muscles pull with forces much bigger than the loads we lift, because they are joined close to the joints.
agreed.evidence: Giovanni Borelli worked this out with the mathematics of levers in a book printed in 1680. Modern doctors have put sensors inside artificial hip joints. During walking, the sensors measure forces of more than twice the body's weight.

agreed.text: Bone gets stronger where it is loaded and weaker where it is not.
agreed.evidence: The serving arm of tennis players has thicker bone than the other arm. Astronauts lose bone from their hips and legs during months in space.

agreed.text: The limbs of all four-limbed vertebrates are built from the same bones.
agreed.evidence: The bones can be matched one by one in skeletons of humans, bats, whales, birds and frogs. They can also be matched in fossils of their ancestors.

challenging.claim: Bones are dry and dead, like stones inside us.
challenging.who: A common idea, because the bones we see in museums and on plates are dry or cooked.
challenging.for: Bone is hard and contains mineral, and a skeleton lasts for hundreds of years after death.
challenging.against: Living bone has cells, blood vessels and nerves. It grows, mends itself and changes with use. A stone does none of these.

challenging.for: 206 is the usual count for a grown-up, and it is a useful number to know.
challenging.against: A newborn has many more separate pieces, which join up later. Some grown-ups have an extra rib or extra small bones in the hands and feet. The number depends on the person and on how you count.

challenging.claim: Cracking your knuckles will give you arthritis, a disease of painful joints.
challenging.for: The pop sounds as if something is being damaged.
challenging.against: An American doctor, Donald Unger, cracked the knuckles of his left hand only, for more than fifty years. He found no arthritis in either hand, and larger studies agree. The pop comes from a gas bubble in the liquid of the joint. Scientists still argue about whether the sound is the bubble forming or collapsing.

challenging.claim: Milk is the only way to get strong bones.
challenging.for: Milk and curd are rich in calcium, and bone needs calcium.
challenging.against: Ragi, sesame seeds, drumstick leaves and small fish eaten whole are also rich in calcium. Bone needs vitamin D from sunlight and the loading of running and jumping as well. Studies that follow large groups of adults do not find clearly fewer broken hips among those who drink more milk.

challenging.claim: The skeleton also sends chemical messages to the rest of the body.
challenging.who: Gerard Karsenty and his team in New York, from 2007.
challenging.for: In mice, bone cells release a substance called osteocalcin into the blood. Mice without it handle sugar badly and store more fat.
challenging.against: Other teams bred mice without osteocalcin and did not see the same changes. How much this matters in humans is not yet known.

challenging.claim: An inside skeleton is a better design than an outside one.
challenging.who: A common idea among humans, who have one.
challenging.for: An endoskeleton grows with the body and can carry very large animals.
challenging.against: Animals with an exoskeleton have lived on Earth for more than 500 million years. More than three out of four known kinds of animal have one. Each plan fits some ways of living.

big_questions.q: Your muscles pull much harder than the weights you lift, and you never feel it. What else does your body do without telling you?
big_questions.hint: In the Ruler Arm experiment the band near the pressed end stretched most. Think about your heart, your gut and your bone cells.

big_questions.q: About one tenth of a grown-up's bone is replaced each year. After many years, is it still the same skeleton?
big_questions.hint: The shape stays, and the material changes. Which one is the skeleton?

big_questions.q: A crab's skeleton protects her from outside. Your skeleton leaves your skin open to the world. Which body feels more of the world?
big_questions.hint: Think about what your skin can feel, and about the hours when a crab is soft after a moult.

big_questions.q: A bat's wing and your arm have the same bones. What does that say about how you and the bat are related?
big_questions.hint: Two families who own the same old cooking pot may share a great-grandmother.

big_questions.q: Astronauts lose bone when their bodies carry no weight. Does a body need the Earth's pull to stay whole?
big_questions.hint: Bone cells build where bone is loaded. On Earth, your own weight loads your legs all day.

big_questions.q: A skeleton can last thousands of years after an animal dies. What can bones tell us about a life, and what can they not tell?
big_questions.hint: Bones can show height, age, old injuries and hard work. Think about what leaves no mark on bone.

story.title: The Dancer Who Was Late for the Drum
story.note: Thangam, Paati, Kamala Chithi and the puppet Mohini are made up. These facts are real: Tamil Nadu has an old string puppet theatre called bommalattam, and Kumbakonam is one of its homes. The muscle that bends the elbow is joined to the forearm close to the elbow. You can feel its tendon in the bend of your arm. In real bommalattam the arms are usually moved with rods. The single finger string here is a simpler puppet, used so that the idea is easy to see.
text: The wooden dancer was called Mohini, and she was always late.

She hung by her strings from a beam in Paati's workroom in Kumbakonam, among kings, demons and a horse with one ear. Paati had carved her from a block of light wood forty years ago, and had repainted her eyes eleven times. Mohini could bow, turn and sway. What she could not do was throw up her right hand on the last beat of the drum.

That hand was Thangam's job. Thangam was nine, and this was the first festival at which Paati had trusted her with a string. It was only one string. It ran from Mohini's right wrist up to a loop on Thangam's finger. In two days the puppets would dance in the temple street, and Kamala Chithi would play the drum. At the end of the dance the drum went tha-dhi-gi-na-thom, and on thom the hand had to be in the air.

It never was. To lift the wooden hand as high as Mohini's head, Thangam had to raise her own hand just as far, the whole length of the puppet's arm. She pulled as fast as she could. The hand floated up after the beat, like someone lifting a pot of water.
"Late," said Chithi from behind the drum.
"I started early that time!"
"Then it was early and slow. A dancer's hand is not carried up. It is thrown."
Thangam looked at Paati, who was painting a demon's teeth and did not look up. "Mohini is not the first dancer with an arm," Paati said. "Go and see how the others are strung."

Thangam went along the beam. The king's string was tied at the wrist. The demon's string was tied at the wrist. Even the horse's front leg was tied just above the hoof. Every arm in the room was strung exactly like Mohini's. She sat down on the step, cross and hot.
Chithi was tightening the drum. Each time she struck it, her hand flew up from the drumskin faster than Thangam's eyes could follow. That hand was never late.

Thangam bent her own arm slowly and watched it. Nothing was tied to her wrist. So what lifted it? She pressed two fingers into the bend of her elbow and bent the arm again. Something rose under her fingertips. It was a cord, hard and tight, as thick as a pencil. It came down from the muscle of her upper arm and went into her forearm two finger-widths below the bend. It did not go to her wrist at all.
Paati had said the others. She had not said the other puppets.

Thangam took Mohini down. She untied the string from the wooden wrist and knotted it round the forearm instead, two finger-widths below the elbow pin. She slipped the loop on her finger and pulled, only a little, the length of her thumb.
Mohini's hand flew up past her painted eyes.
"Again," said Chithi, and played. Tha-dhi-gi-na-thom. On thom the hand was there. Thangam laughed out loud. She did it again, and again. On the fourth pull the string snapped, and the hand dropped.

She looked at the broken end. Her finger hurt too. There was a red line where the loop had bitten into it. That same thread had lifted that same hand a hundred times from the wrist, and it had never broken.

Now Paati put down her brush. "A small pull for a long throw," she said. "Did you think it would cost nothing? Where you have tied it now, the string must pull many times harder than the hand weighs. Feel your own cord again. Is it a sewing thread?"
Thangam felt it. It was the hardest thing in her arm that was not bone.

Paati opened a tin and took out a length of thick waxed cord. She cut a small notch in the wooden forearm so that the cord would not slip. She wound a strip of soft cloth round Thangam's finger. "Your body paid that price long before any puppet maker did," she said. "It does not complain, so nobody notices."

On the festival evening the street smelled of jasmine and hot oil. The lamps were lit, and the kings and demons came down on their strings. Mohini bowed, turned and swayed. At the last line of the song the drum ran tha-dhi-gi-na, and Thangam's finger moved the length of her thumb.
Thom. Mohini's hand was in the air, exactly on the beat. A small boy in the front row threw up his own hand to match.

Afterwards Chithi gave Thangam a steel tumbler of buttermilk. As she lifted it to drink, she put two fingers of her other hand into the bend of her elbow. The cord rose and went tight. It had pulled like that every day of her life, and she had not once felt it.
story.epiphany: A string tied at the wrist must be pulled a long way, so the hand is slow. A string tied near the elbow needs only a short pull, so the hand is fast. But the string must pull much harder. Thangam finds that her own arm is strung near the elbow.
ask: Why does a hand move faster when the string is tied near the elbow, not at the wrist?
Why does a string tied near the elbow have to be stronger?
Press into the bend of your own elbow and bend your arm. How far from the bend is the cord you feel?
