games.title: Inside, Outside or None? The skeleton cards
games.context: This is a card game about the skeletons of real animals. Each card describes an animal. You say whether the skeleton is inside the body, outside the body, or not hard at all.

setup.art: Twenty cards in a shuffled pile on a table, with three small tokens marked Inside, Outside and None in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while another player slides one token forward, face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the front. Everyone else puts down one token, face down.

setup.art: The tokens turned face up and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the back.

printables.title: 20 animal cards: an animal on the front, the kind of skeleton and a fact on the back

items.f: A house crow, who flies up to the roof with a piece of roti.
items.b: Inside. Many of a bird's bones are hollow and have air in them, which keeps the bird light.

items.f: A cockroach, who runs under the kitchen shelf.
items.b: Outside. A young cockroach moults several times as she grows.

items.f: An earthworm, who comes up from wet soil after rain.
items.b: None. An earthworm's body is a row of rings filled with liquid, and the muscles squeeze against the liquid.

items.f: A mud crab, sold alive in a fish market.
items.b: Outside. A crab's hard coat has chalky mineral in it as well as chitin.

items.f: A house gecko, who walks on the wall near the tube light.
items.b: Inside. A gecko has a skull, a backbone, ribs and four limbs with the same bones as yours.

items.f: A jellyfish, who drifts in the sea off the coast.
items.b: None. A jellyfish is mostly water held in a soft jelly, and out of the water the body flattens.

items.f: A rohu fish, who swims in a river.
items.b: Inside. A fish has a skull, a backbone and many fine bones that hold the muscles.

items.f: A black ant, who carries a grain of sugar.
items.b: Outside. An ant's muscles are inside the hard tubes of her legs.

items.f: An octopus, who hides in a crack in a reef.
items.b: None. Her only hard part is a beak, so she can squeeze through very small holes.

items.f: A star tortoise, who pulls her head into her shell.
items.b: Inside. The shell is made from her ribs and backbone. It is part of her skeleton, and she cannot leave it.

items.f: A garden snail, who climbs a wet wall.
items.b: Outside. The shell is a hard outside part. A snail does not moult, and adds to the rim of the shell while growing.

items.f: A shark, who swims in the open sea.
items.b: Inside. A shark's skeleton is made of cartilage, the bendy material in your ear, with no bone.

items.f: A house spider, who waits in the corner of a window.
items.b: Outside. A spider moults, and you may find the empty coat hanging in the web.

items.f: An elephant, who walks through a forest in Kerala.
items.b: Inside. An elephant's leg bones stand almost straight, like pillars, to carry her weight.

items.f: A prawn, who swims backwards with a flick of the tail.
items.b: Outside. The thin shell you peel off a prawn is the exoskeleton.

items.f: A fruit bat, who hangs in a banyan tree.
items.b: Inside. The long thin bones in a bat's wing are finger bones.

items.f: A scorpion, who hides under a stone in dry country.
items.b: Outside. A scorpion's claws, legs and tail are all jointed tubes of hard coat.

items.f: A starfish, who clings to a rock in a tide pool.
items.b: Inside. A starfish has thousands of tiny hard plates under the skin.

items.f: A slug, who leaves a shiny trail on a leaf.
items.b: None. A slug is a relative of snails and has no shell on the outside.

items.f: A human child, who is playing this game.
items.b: Inside. You have about 206 bones, and more than half are in your hands and feet.

printables.title: 3 skeleton tokens: Inside, Outside, None. Make one set for each player

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts one token face down: Inside, Outside or None. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the first word on the back scores 1 point.
A player who also gives one gain or one cost of that kind of skeleton scores 1 more point. The reader decides.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone? Read a card, say the kind of skeleton aloud, then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right answer.
After all 20 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 20 is your result.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player one set of three tokens.
flow.say: Each card describes a real animal. Your three tokens are three kinds of skeleton: inside the body, outside the body, and none that is hard.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take three tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Inside, Outside or None. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first ten cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card five.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Choose a token and put it face down. Now turn it over. The reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: How did you decide where the animal's hard parts are?
good: I thought about what I would feel if I touched the animal.
A hard coat on the outside means an exoskeleton.
Soft skin with hard parts under it means the skeleton is inside.

flow.parent: A useful question for a stuck child is: if you pressed this animal gently, would you feel something hard at once, or soft skin first? One child can play alone or with you.
flow.context: In this step of Inside, Outside or None you play the first ten animal cards.

flow.do: Play the last ten cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Ten more cards. This time, also try to give one gain or one cost of that kind of skeleton. A good one earns one more point.
flow.kid: Play ten more cards. Give one gain or cost each time.
flow.context: In this step of Inside, Outside or None you play the last ten cards. You also give a gain or a cost of each skeleton.

flow.do: Count the points. Then sort all 20 cards into three piles by kind of skeleton and look at the piles.
flow.say: Let us sort the cards into three piles. Which pile holds the biggest animals? Which animals have to moult?
flow.kid: Sort the cards into three piles. Which pile has the biggest animals?

check.q: Which kind of skeleton must be shed and replaced for the animal to grow?
options: A body with no hard skeleton
check.why: A hard coat on the outside cannot stretch, so the old coat is split and a bigger one grows. Bones inside the body grow along with the body. If you chose the endoskeleton, remember that you have never shed your bones.

flow.context: This is the last step of Inside, Outside or None. You sort the animal cards by kind of skeleton and compare the piles.

games.title: Which Muscle Pulled? A moving game
games.context: This is a game you play with your own body. Each card names a movement. You point to the place where you think the pulling muscle is. Then you do the movement and feel for it.

setup.art: Twelve small cards in a pile, the top one reading 'Bend your elbow'.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 12 movement cards. Shuffle them into a pile.

setup.art: A child pointing with one finger at the front of her own upper arm before moving.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. First point to where you think the pulling muscle is.

setup.art: The child bending her elbow slowly with her other hand resting on the front of her upper arm.
setup.caption: 3. Do the movement slowly. Feel which place goes hard. Then read the back.

printables.title: 12 movement cards: a movement on the front, the place of the pulling muscle on the back

items.f: Bend your elbow, as if lifting a tumbler to your mouth.
items.b: The front of the upper arm. This muscle is the biceps.

items.f: Put your palm on a table and press down hard.
items.b: The back of the upper arm. This muscle is the triceps, and it straightens the elbow.

items.f: Stand and rise onto your toes.
items.b: The back of the lower leg. The calf muscles pull the heel up.

items.f: Stand on your heels and lift your toes off the floor.
items.b: The front of the lower leg, just beside the shin bone.

items.f: Sit on a chair and lift one foot until the leg is straight.
items.b: The front of the thigh. These muscles straighten the knee.

items.f: Stand and bring one heel up towards your bottom.
items.b: The back of the thigh. These muscles bend the knee.

items.f: Bite your back teeth together firmly.
items.b: The cheek, just in front of the corner of the jaw. This muscle closes the jaw.

items.f: Squeeze your hand into a tight fist.
items.b: The palm side of the forearm. The muscles that close your fingers are in the forearm.

items.f: Lift one arm straight out to the side.
items.b: The top of the shoulder. This muscle lifts the arm.

items.f: Lie on your back and lift your head and shoulders.
items.b: The front of the belly. These muscles bend the body forward.

items.f: Lift both shoulders towards your ears.
items.b: Between the neck and the shoulder, on each side.

items.f: Rest your arm palm down on a table and lift only the hand.
items.b: The top of the forearm. These muscles bend the wrist back.

printables.title: Score sheet: 12 movements
items: Movement 1 to 6: put a tick for each right place ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___
Movement 7 to 12: put a tick for each right place ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___

rules: Take the top card and read the movement aloud. Keep the back hidden.
Before anyone moves, every player points to the place on their own body where they think the pulling muscle is.
Now everyone does the movement slowly and feels with the other hand for the place that goes hard.
Read the back. Every player who pointed to the right place scores 1 point.
A player who can also find the partner muscle, the one that undoes the movement, scores 1 more point.
Playing alone? Point, move, feel, then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right place.
After all 12 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, try to beat your score next time.

flow.do: Cut out the 12 cards and shuffle them. Clear a space where everyone can stand, sit and lie down.
flow.say: Each card names a movement. A muscle somewhere on your body pulls to make it happen. We will point first, then move and feel.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Make space to move.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Muscle Pulled. You set up the cards and make space.

flow.do: Play the first six cards by the rules. Move slowly each time, and hold the end of the movement for a count of three.
flow.say: Point first. Now move slowly and hold. Put your other hand where you pointed. Did that place go hard, or was it somewhere else?
flow.kid: Point first. Move slowly. Feel which place goes hard.
flow.parent: A muscle that is pulling feels hard and thick. A relaxed muscle feels soft. If your child cannot feel a change, push gently against the movement so the muscle has to work harder.
flow.context: In this step of Which Muscle Pulled you play the first six movement cards.

flow.do: Play the last six cards. For each one, also look for the partner muscle that undoes the movement.
flow.say: Six more cards. After each one, undo the movement slowly. Where is the muscle that pulls you back?
flow.kid: Play six more cards. Find the muscle that undoes each movement.

ask.q: Where is the partner muscle usually found?
good: On the opposite side of the same bone.
If one is at the front, the other is at the back.

flow.context: In this step of Which Muscle Pulled you play the last six cards and look for each partner muscle.

flow.do: Count the points. Talk about the question below.
flow.say: The muscles that close your fist are in your forearm, not in your fingers. How does their pull reach your fingers?
flow.kid: Count your points. How does a forearm muscle move a finger?

check.q: A muscle at the front of a bone bends a joint. Where is the muscle that straightens it?
options: On the opposite side of the bone
check.why: A muscle can only pull. So a second muscle on the opposite side has to pull the bone back. If you chose 'inside the same muscle', remember that a muscle cannot push.

flow.parent: Long tendons run from the forearm muscles through the wrist to the finger bones. Your child can see them move on the back of the hand when they wiggle their fingers.
flow.context: This is the last step of Which Muscle Pulled. You count the points and talk about how a muscle can move a bone far away.

experiments.title: The Ruler Arm: does it matter where the muscle is tied?
experiments.question: A ruler is a model forearm with coins at the hand end. A rubber band lifts it from 5, 15 or 25 centimetres from the elbow end. At which place does the band stretch most? At which place is the band lifted the shortest distance?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. At which of the three places will the rubber band stretch the most? At which place will you lift the band the shortest distance? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same ruler, the same five coins and the same rubber band every time. Lift the coin end to the same mark each time, 12 centimetres above the table. Pull straight up, and measure only when everything is still. Try each place twice, because one try can be a fluke. Only one thing changes: the place where the band is tied.
results_table: Where the band is tied (centimetres from the elbow end)
Length of the stretched band in centimetres: try 1 and try 2
Height of the thread loop above the table in centimetres: try 1 and try 2

materials.item: a 30 centimetre ruler, wooden or stiff plastic. This is the forearm
a second ruler or a measuring tape
a thin rubber band
a piece of thread or thin string, about 30 centimetres long
coins of the same kind, taped in a stack
sticky tape
a tall water bottle, to carry the 12 centimetre mark
a pencil and a notebook page for the results

experiments.record: Draw a table with three rows, for 25, 15 and 5 centimetres. For each place, write the length of the stretched band and the height of the loop, for both tries. Write the length of the loose band above the table.
experiments.context: In this experiment a ruler is a model forearm. You lift it with a rubber band tied at three places. You measure how hard and how far the band has to pull.

setup.art: A wooden ruler lying flat on a table with a stack of five coins taped on top at the 30 centimetre end, and a child's finger pressing down on the 0 end.
setup.caption: 1. Tape five coins on the 30 centimetre end. Press a finger on the 0 end. That end is the elbow.

setup.art: A loop of thread tied round the ruler at the 25 centimetre mark, with a rubber band hooked through the loop.
setup.caption: 2. Tie a thread loop round the ruler. Hook the rubber band through the loop.

setup.art: A water bottle standing next to the coin end of the ruler, with a strip of tape on the bottle 12 centimetres above the table.
setup.caption: 3. Stick tape on a bottle, 12 centimetres above the table. Stand the bottle by the coins.

setup.art: A child pulling the rubber band straight up so that the coin end of the ruler is level with the tape on the bottle, while a grown-up holds a second ruler beside the stretched band.
setup.caption: 4. Lift by the band until the coin end reaches the tape. Measure the band and the height of the loop.

setup.art: The same ruler with the thread loop moved to the 5 centimetre mark, the band stretched long and the loop only a little above the table.
setup.caption: 5. Move the loop to 15 centimetres, then to 5 centimetres. Measure again each time.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results. The loose band was 6 centimetres long

flow.do: Show your child the ruler, the coins and the rubber band. Explain the three tying places. Ask for both guesses and the reasons, and write them down.
flow.say: This ruler is a forearm. The coins are a load in the hand. The rubber band is the muscle. Where will the band stretch most: at 5, 15 or 25 centimetres? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The ruler is an arm. The band is a muscle. Where will the band stretch most? Why?

ask.q: At which place will you have to lift the band the shortest distance? Why?
good: Near the elbow end, because that part of the ruler hardly rises.
At the coin end, because it is nearest the load.
Any guess with a reason.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children expect the band to stretch most when it is tied at the coins. That is where the weight is.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ruler Arm experiment. You guess which tying place will stretch the rubber band most, before you test.

flow.do: Tape the five coins in a stack on top of the 30 centimetre end. Tie the thread in a loose loop round the ruler and hook the band through it. Stick tape on the bottle 12 centimetres above the table. Measure the loose band and write its length.
flow.say: Let us build the arm. The coins go on the hand end. The band hooks into this loop of thread. First we measure the band while nothing is pulling it.
flow.kid: Tape on the coins. Tie the loop. Mark the bottle. Measure the loose band.
flow.parent: The loop must be loose enough to slide along the ruler and tight enough not to fall off. A small piece of tape holds it at each mark. Lay the band flat and straight to measure it, without pulling.
flow.context: In this step of the Ruler Arm experiment you build the model arm. You also measure the rubber band before it is stretched.

flow.do: Slide the loop to the 25 centimetre mark and tape it there. Your child presses one finger on the 0 end and lifts the band straight up with the other hand. They stop when the coin end is level with the tape on the bottle. Measure the band, then the height of the loop above the table. Do it twice.
flow.say: Press the elbow end down. Lift the band slowly until the coins reach the tape mark. Hold still. I will measure the band and then the height of the loop.
flow.kid: Press the elbow end. Lift until the coins reach the tape. Hold still.
flow.parent: Measure the band from the thread loop to the finger that holds it. Measure the loop height from the table top to the ruler at the loop.
flow.context: In this step of the Ruler Arm experiment the rubber band is tied at 25 centimetres, close to the coins.

flow.do: Move the loop to the 15 centimetre mark and tape it. Lift to the same tape mark, twice. Measure the band and the loop height each time.
flow.say: Now the band is tied at the middle of the forearm. Lift the coins to the same mark. Does the band feel different in your fingers?
flow.kid: Move the loop to 15 centimetres. Lift again. Measure again.
flow.context: In this step of the Ruler Arm experiment the rubber band is tied at the middle of the ruler.

flow.do: Move the loop to the 5 centimetre mark and tape it. Lift to the same tape mark, twice. Measure the band and the loop height each time.
flow.say: Now the band is tied close to the elbow. Press the elbow end firmly, because it will try to jump up. Lift the coins to the same mark.
flow.kid: Move the loop to 5 centimetres. Press hard on the elbow end. Lift again.

check.q: In the Ruler Arm experiment, why do you lift the coins to the same tape mark every time?
options: So only the tying place changes
So the band does not break
check.why: A fair test changes one thing only. Suppose the coins went higher on some tries. Then you could not tell whether the tying place or the height had changed the result.

flow.parent: The band may hardly stretch more at 5 centimetres than at 25. If so, tape on five more coins or use a thinner band. Then repeat all three places. If the band looks ready to snap, use fewer coins.
flow.context: In this step of the Ruler Arm experiment the rubber band is tied 5 centimetres from the elbow end.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your numbers. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. The coins never changed. So why did the band stretch more at one place?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: What did you gain by tying the band close to the elbow end?
good: A short lift of the band moved the coins a long way.
The loop rose only about 2 centimetres, and the coins rose 12.
The band had to pull much harder.
The band stretched the most there.
The elbow end pushed up hard against my finger.

flow.parent: In most homes the band is longest when tied at 5 centimetres and shortest at 25. The loop height is about 10, 6 and 2 centimetres. Write down what you really found. The reason: the ruler is a lever that turns at the pressed end. A pull close to that end has to be much bigger to hold up the same load. At 5 centimetres the pull is about five times as big as at 25. In return, the band moves only one fifth as far for the same rise of the coins.
flow.context: In this step of the Ruler Arm experiment you say what your measurements show about the three tying places.

flow.do: Your child bends one elbow and presses two fingers of the other hand into the bend. They bend and straighten the arm slowly and feel the cord there. Ask which tying place on the ruler is most like their own arm.
flow.say: Press two fingers into the bend of your elbow. Bend your arm slowly. Can you feel a tight cord? That is the tendon of your biceps. How far is it from the bend?
flow.kid: Press into the bend of your elbow. Bend your arm. Feel the cord.
flow.think: Your muscle is tied like the band at 5 centimetres. What does that tell you about how hard it pulls?
flow.parent: The biceps tendon joins the forearm about 3 centimetres from a child's elbow, and about 4 from a grown-up's. That is like the 5 centimetre place on the ruler, or closer. So the muscle pulls several times harder than the load in the hand.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Ruler Arm experiment. You find the tendon in your own elbow and compare your arm with the ruler.

experiments.title: The Paper Ice Test: why does a bone not shatter?
experiments.question: Two slabs of ice are made the same size. One is plain ice. The other is ice with torn newspaper frozen inside it. Which slab breaks from a lower drop?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which slab will break first when you drop them: the plain ice or the paper ice? Or will they break at the same height? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two plates of the same size and fill both to the same depth, 1 centimetre. Freeze them side by side for the same time. Drop both slabs flat, from the same heights, onto the same floor. Only one thing changes: the paper in the ice. One try can be a fluke. If your freezer has room, make two slabs of each kind.
results_table: Plain ice: whole, cracked or in pieces?
Paper ice: whole, cracked or in pieces?

materials.item: small steel plates with a rim, or flat steel lids, of the same size
full pages of old newspaper
a bowl of water for soaking the paper
a ruler
a freezer with a flat shelf
an old towel, to hold the cold slabs and to dry the floor
a pencil and a notebook page for the results

experiments.safety: Do the drops on a bathroom or balcony floor, with a grown-up. Wet floors are slippery, so dry the floor at the end. Put the melted paper in the dustbin, not down the drain.

schedule.what: Guess, make the plain slab and the paper slab, and put both in the freezer.
Take the slabs out, drop them from four heights, and say what the results show.

experiments.record: Draw a table with four rows, for drops from 10, 20, 40 and 80 centimetres. For each slab, write 'whole', 'cracked' or 'in pieces' after every drop.
experiments.context: In this experiment you freeze a slab of plain ice and a slab of ice with torn paper in it. You drop both to find out what fibres do for a hard material. Bone is a hard mineral with fibres in it.

setup.art: A child tearing newspaper into small pieces over a bowl of water, with two identical small steel plates beside the bowl.
setup.caption: 1. Tear two newspaper pages into pieces smaller than a stamp. Soak them for 10 minutes.

setup.art: Two steel plates side by side: one holding clear water, the other holding grey paper mush just covered with water, and a ruler standing in the first plate.
setup.caption: 2. Fill one plate with water, 1 centimetre deep. Fill the other with paper mush and water to the same depth.

setup.art: The two plates lying flat on a freezer shelf.
setup.caption: 3. Freeze both plates flat until the next day.

setup.art: A grown-up and a child on a bathroom floor, the child holding a round slab of ice flat at the height of a ruler's 20 centimetre mark, ready to drop it.
setup.caption: 4. Drop each slab flat from 10, 20, 40 and 80 centimetres. Write what happens.

flow.do: Day 1. Show your child the plates and the newspaper. Explain the test. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will freeze two slabs of ice. One is plain. One has torn newspaper inside. Tomorrow we drop them. Which will break first, and why do you think so?
flow.kid: One slab is plain ice. One has paper inside. Which breaks first? Why?
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Some children expect the paper to make the ice weaker, because wet paper is weak.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Paper Ice Test. You guess which slab of ice will break first, before you make them.

flow.do: Tear the two pages into pieces smaller than a stamp. Soak them in the bowl for 10 minutes, then rub them into a mush. Pour water into the first plate, 1 centimetre deep. Spread the mush in the second plate and add water until it is just covered, 1 centimetre deep. Put both plates flat in the freezer.
flow.say: Tear the paper small and soak it. Now rub it between your fingers until it is a mush. The mush goes in one plate. Plain water goes in the other. Both must be the same depth.
flow.kid: Tear the paper small. Soak it and rub it to mush. Fill both plates. Freeze them.
flow.parent: Check the depth with the ruler. Press the mush down so that no dry paper sticks out. If the plates do not fit flat in the freezer, use two smaller steel lids.
flow.context: In this step of the Paper Ice Test you make one plate of plain water and one of paper mush. Both go in the freezer.

flow.do: Day 2. Take both plates out. Dip the bottom of each plate in tap water for about 20 seconds. Slide the slabs out onto the towel. Let your child hold each slab in the towel and look at it against the light.
flow.say: Here are yesterday's slabs. Hold each one in the towel. Look through it at the window. What do you notice about each?
flow.kid: Take the slabs out. Hold each in the towel. What do you notice?
flow.wait: Freeze the plates for at least 8 hours, until the next day
flow.context: In this step of the Paper Ice Test you take the two frozen slabs out of their plates.

flow.do: Go to a bathroom or balcony floor. Stand the ruler on the floor. Your child holds the plain slab flat at the 10 centimetre mark and lets go. Write whole, cracked or in pieces. Do the same with the paper slab. Repeat from 20 and 40 centimetres, and from 80 centimetres measured against a wall. Stop dropping a slab once it is in pieces.
flow.say: Hold the slab flat, level with the mark, and just let go. Do not throw it. What happened to the plain slab? Now the paper slab, from the same height.
flow.kid: Drop each slab flat from each height. Write what happens each time.

check.q: In the Paper Ice Test, why must both slabs be the same thickness?
options: So only the paper is different
So they fit in the plate
check.why: A thick slab is harder to break than a thin one. If one slab were thicker, you could not tell whether the thickness or the paper had made the difference.

flow.parent: Work quickly, because ice gets weaker as it melts. The plain slab may still be whole after 80 centimetres. If so, hit each slab in the middle with the back of a heavy spoon. Count the hits until it breaks.
flow.context: In this step of the Paper Ice Test you drop the plain slab and the paper slab from four heights.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below. Then dry the floor.
flow.say: Look at your table. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Look at the broken edge of each slab. What is different?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: What do you see at a crack in the paper ice?
good: Paper fibres going across the crack.
The two sides are still held together.
It looks hairy, not smooth.

ask.q: Which part of a bone is like the ice, and which is like the paper?
good: The hard mineral is like the ice.
The collagen fibres are like the paper.

flow.parent: In most homes the plain slab cracks or breaks from 20 to 40 centimetres. The paper slab usually stays in one piece from every height, though it may crack. Write down what you really found. The reason: ice is hard, but once a crack starts it runs straight through. In the paper ice, thousands of fibres lie across the path of any crack and hold the two sides together. Bone is built in a similar way. The mineral in bone is hard and would crack like ice. The collagen fibres stop cracks from running through.
flow.think: Wet paper alone is floppy, and ice alone shatters. What does that tell you about a bone with too little mineral, or too little collagen?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Paper Ice Test. You say what the drops show about the plain slab and the paper slab.

activities.title: Bone Labels: name twelve bones on a real body

materials.item: small slips of paper, each about as long as a finger
sticky tape, or a little cooked rice to use as paste
a pencil
a grown-up or an older child to be the model

schedule.what: Write twelve bone names, stick each one on the right place on a model, and say what each bone does.

activities.record: Write the twelve bone names in your notebook. Next to each, write one job: holds up, protects, or helps to move. A bone can have more than one job.
activities.context: In this activity you write the names of twelve bones on slips of paper. You stick each one on the right place on a real person. Then you say what each bone does.

setup.art: Twelve paper slips on a table with bone names written on them in pencil: skull, lower jaw, collarbone, shoulder blade, breastbone, ribs, backbone, humerus, radius and ulna, pelvis, femur, tibia.
setup.caption: 1. Write one bone name on each of twelve slips.

setup.art: A child feeling her own collarbone with her fingers while holding a paper slip in the other hand.
setup.caption: 2. Find each bone on your own body first. Press gently and feel it.

setup.art: A smiling grown-up standing still with paper slips stuck on her clothes at the shoulder, chest, arm, hip and thigh, and a child sticking one more on her shin.
setup.caption: 3. Stick each slip on the model, right over that bone.

flow.do: Write these names on the twelve slips: skull, lower jaw, collarbone, shoulder blade, breastbone, ribs, backbone, humerus, radius and ulna, pelvis, femur, tibia. Read each name aloud together.
flow.say: Here are twelve bone names. Some are everyday words and some are the names doctors use. Before I tell you anything, which of these can you already find on your own body?
flow.kid: Write twelve bone names on twelve slips. Which ones do you know already?
flow.parent: The humerus is the upper arm bone. The radius and the ulna are the two forearm bones. The pelvis is the ring of hip bones. The femur is the thigh bone. The tibia is the shin bone.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bone Labels. You write the names of twelve bones on slips of paper.

flow.do: For each slip, your child first finds the bone on their own body by pressing gently. Then they stick the slip on the model over the same bone. Help only after they have tried.
flow.say: Take one slip. Find that bone on yourself first. Press gently. What shape is it? Now stick the slip on me, right over the same bone.
flow.kid: Find each bone on yourself. Then stick the slip on the model.

ask.q: What do you notice about the forearm when you turn your palm up and down?
good: There are two bones.
One bone seems to roll over the other.

flow.parent: The shoulder blade is the flat bone on the upper back. It sticks out when the arm is pulled behind the back. The breastbone is the flat bone down the middle of the chest.
flow.context: In this step of Bone Labels you find each of the twelve bones on your own body. Then you label it on a model.

flow.do: Point to each slip in turn. Your child says what that bone does: holds the body up, protects something soft, or helps to move. For the bones that protect, they name the organ behind them.
flow.say: Look at the labels. Which bones have something soft and important behind them? What is it? Which bones carry your weight when you stand?
flow.kid: Point to each label. What does that bone do? What does it protect?

check.q: Which bones make a cage round the heart and the lungs?
options: The skull and the lower jaw
check.why: Twelve pairs of ribs curve from the backbone to the front, where most join the breastbone. The heart and lungs lie inside. If you chose the skull, remember that the skull guards the brain.

flow.parent: The skull protects the brain. The ribs and breastbone protect the heart and lungs. The backbone protects the spinal cord. The pelvis protects the bladder and lower gut. The backbone, pelvis, femur and tibia carry the body's weight.
flow.context: This is the last step of Bone Labels. You say what each of the twelve labelled bones does.

activities.title: Thigh Bone and Height: how many thigh bones tall are you?

materials.item: a ball of string or wool
scissors
a measuring tape or a ruler
three or more people of different heights
a pencil and a notebook page

schedule.what: Cut a string as long as each person is tall and fold it in four. Compare it with that person's thigh bone.

activities.record: A table with one row for each person. Write their height, the length of their thigh bone, and how many thigh bones fit into their height.
activities.context: In this activity you measure the height and the thigh bone of three people at home. You find out how many times the thigh bone fits into the height.

setup.art: A child standing against a wall while a grown-up holds a string from the floor to the top of her head.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a string as long as the person is tall.

setup.art: Hands folding a long string in half and then in half again.
setup.caption: 2. Fold the string in half, and in half again. Now it is one quarter of the height.

setup.art: A grown-up standing with one hand on the bony bump at the side of the hip, while a child holds the folded string from that bump down to the knee.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the folded string from the hip bump to the knee joint. Compare.

flow.do: Help your child find the top of the thigh bone. They stand, press a hand on the side of the hip and swing that leg. A hard bump moves under the hand. Then they find the bottom end, at the outer side of the knee joint. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: Your thigh bone runs from this bump at your hip to your knee. It is your longest bone. How many thigh bones tall do you think you are? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Find the bump at your hip. Find your knee. How many thigh bones tall are you?
flow.context: This is the first step of Thigh Bone and Height. You find the two ends of your thigh bone and guess how many times it fits into your height.

flow.do: For each person, cut a string as long as they are tall. Fold it in half twice. Hold the folded string along their thigh, from the hip bump to the knee joint. Note whether it is longer, shorter or about the same. Then measure the height and the thigh bone in centimetres and write both down.
flow.say: Stand straight against the wall. I will cut a string as long as you are tall. Now fold it in four. Is one quarter of you as long as your thigh bone?
flow.kid: Cut a string as tall as you. Fold it in four. Compare it with your thigh.
flow.parent: For most people the folded string is close to the thigh bone, within about three finger-widths. Measuring through clothes and muscle is rough, so small differences do not matter.
flow.context: In this step of Thigh Bone and Height you compare one quarter of each person's height with their thigh bone.

flow.do: Look at the table. Talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Was the thigh bone close to a quarter of the height for everyone? A scientist finds one thigh bone in the ground. What could she work out about the person?
flow.kid: Was the thigh bone about a quarter each time? What could one bone tell a scientist?

ask.q: How could you estimate a person's height from the thigh bone alone?
good: Multiply the length of the thigh bone by about 4.
Four thigh bones make about one height.

check.q: A thigh bone is 40 centimetres long. About how tall was the person?
check.why: A thigh bone is about a quarter of a person's height. 4 times 40 is 160. If you chose 80, you doubled the bone once, and it needs doubling twice.

flow.parent: This really is done. In the 1950s the American scientist Mildred Trotter measured the bones of several thousand people whose heights were known. She worked out rules for finding height from a thigh bone. Her rules are more exact than 'four times', and they are still used.
flow.context: This is the last step of Thigh Bone and Height. You look for a pattern in the measurements of three people.

activities.title: Lift and Press: two muscles for one elbow

materials.item: a heavy table, a kitchen counter or a stone window sill
a piece of string about 50 centimetres long
a matchbox or a small empty tumbler

schedule.what: Feel which arm muscle goes hard when you lift and when you press. Then try to push a matchbox with a string.

activities.record: Draw your arm twice. In the first drawing you are lifting, and in the second you are pressing down. Colour the muscle that was hard in each drawing.
activities.context: In this activity you lift up under a table and then press down on top of it. You feel which muscle of your upper arm does each job. You find out why one muscle is not enough.

setup.art: A child sitting at a heavy table with one hand palm up under the table top, lifting, and the other hand holding the front of that upper arm.
setup.caption: 1. Put one palm under the table and lift gently. Feel the front and the back of your upper arm.

setup.art: The same child with the palm flat on top of the table, pressing down, and the other hand holding the back of that upper arm.
setup.caption: 2. Put your palm on top and press down. Feel the front and the back again.

setup.art: A matchbox on a table with a string tied to it, the string lying slack in a curve as a child tries to push the box with it.
setup.caption: 3. Tie a string to a matchbox. Pull the box with the string. Then try to push it with the string.

flow.do: Your child sits at the table and puts one hand under the table top, palm up. They lift gently, as if to raise the table, and hold for a count of five. With the other hand they feel the front of the upper arm, then the back.
flow.say: Lift up gently and hold. Feel the front of your upper arm with your other hand. Now feel the back. Which is hard and which is soft?
flow.kid: Lift up under the table. Feel the front of your arm. Feel the back.
flow.parent: The front muscle, the biceps, is hard and the back muscle is soft. The table must be too heavy to lift. A gentle effort is enough.
flow.context: This is the first step of Lift and Press. You lift up under a table and feel which muscle of your upper arm goes hard.

flow.do: Now your child puts the same palm flat on top of the table. They press down for a count of five. They feel the front and the back of the upper arm again.
flow.say: Now press down on the table and hold. Feel the front and the back again. What has changed?
flow.kid: Press down on the table. Feel the front and the back again.

ask.q: Why does your arm need a second muscle at the back?
good: The front muscle can only bend the elbow.
Something else has to pull the arm straight.

flow.parent: This time the back muscle, the triceps, is hard and the biceps is soft.
flow.context: In this step of Lift and Press you press down on a table. You feel which muscle of your upper arm goes hard.

flow.do: Tie the string to the matchbox. Your child pulls the box across the table with the string. Then they try to push the box away using only the string. Talk about the question below.
flow.say: Pull the box with the string. That works. Now push the box away with the string. What happens? How is a muscle like this string?
flow.kid: Pull the box with the string. Now try to push with the string.

check.q: Why do muscles work in pairs?
options: A muscle can pull but cannot push
Two muscles are lighter than one
check.why: A muscle moves a bone by getting shorter. It cannot get longer by itself and push the bone back. So another muscle on the opposite side pulls the bone the other way.

flow.context: This is the last step of Lift and Press. You find that a string can pull but not push, and compare it with a muscle.

activities.title: Bendy Bone: take the mineral out of a bone (if your family cooks chicken)

materials.item: thin chicken bones of the same kind, cleaned of meat. Wing bones work best
glass tumblers or jars
vinegar, enough to cover one bone, about one cup
water, enough to cover the other bone
two plates to cover the tumblers

activities.safety: Wash your hands with soap after touching the bones. Keep the tumblers out of reach of small children and pets, and throw the bones away at the end.

schedule.what: Test both bones for stiffness, then put one in vinegar and one in water.
Take both bones out, rinse them and try to bend them. Put them back.
Test both bones again and say what the vinegar took away.

activities.record: A table with two rows, for the vinegar bone and the water bone. Write 'stiff', 'a little bendy' or 'very bendy' for day 1, day 3 and day 5.
activities.context: This activity is for families who cook chicken. You leave one chicken bone in vinegar and one in water for five days. You see what a bone is like when its mineral is taken out.

setup.art: Two clean, thin chicken bones on a plate next to two glass tumblers.
setup.caption: 1. Clean two thin chicken bones. Try to bend each one gently.

setup.art: Two glass tumblers, each with one bone inside, one labelled Vinegar and one labelled Water, each covered with a small plate.
setup.caption: 2. Cover one bone with vinegar and the other with water. Cover the tumblers.

setup.art: A child's hands bending a thin bone into a curve.
setup.caption: 3. On day 3 and day 5, rinse the bones and try to bend them again.

flow.do: Day 1. Let your child try gently to bend each bone, and write down 'stiff'. Put one bone in each tumbler. Cover one with vinegar and the other with water. Cover the tumblers with plates and label them. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: Both bones are stiff now. Vinegar is a weak acid. One bone will sit in vinegar and one in water for five days. What do you think will happen to each? Why?
flow.kid: Try to bend each bone. Put one in vinegar and one in water. What will happen?
flow.parent: Cooked bones from a curry work as well as raw ones. Thin bones change fastest. Small bubbles on the vinegar bone are normal.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Bendy Bone. You test two chicken bones and put one in vinegar and one in water.

flow.do: Day 3. Take out both bones, rinse them under the tap and let your child try to bend each one. Write the result. Put the bones back.
flow.say: Two days have passed. Rinse the bones. Try to bend each one gently. Is there any difference yet?
flow.kid: Rinse both bones. Try to bend them. Write what you find.
flow.wait: Do this two days after you put the bones in
flow.context: This is day 3 of Bendy Bone. You check the bone in vinegar and the bone in water.

flow.do: Day 5. Rinse and test both bones again. Write the results. Talk about the questions below, then throw the bones away and wash hands.
flow.say: Rinse the bones and bend them once more. The bone still has its shape. So what did the vinegar take out, and what is left?
flow.kid: Bend both bones again. What did the vinegar take out? What is left?
flow.wait: Do this four days after you put the bones in

ask.q: Why did we keep one bone in water?
good: To check that the vinegar made the change, not just soaking.
So we have something to compare with.

check.q: A bone kept in vinegar goes bendy. What has the vinegar removed?
check.why: The acid in vinegar dissolves the calcium mineral. The collagen fibres are left, and they bend like rubber. The bone in water keeps its mineral and stays stiff.

flow.parent: The vinegar bone usually bends easily by day 5. A very thin one can be tied in a loose knot. If it is still stiff, change the vinegar and wait three more days. The bone in water stays stiff.
flow.context: This is day 5 of Bendy Bone. You compare the bone from the vinegar with the bone from the water.

activities.title: Shell or Stone: where should the hard part go?

materials.item: a thing with the hard part outside: a groundnut in the shell, a cardamom pod or a whole coconut
a thing with the hard part inside: a date, a mango, a jamun or a piece of tamarind with the seed
a pencil and a notebook page

schedule.what: Compare a hard-outside thing with a hard-inside thing, as models of two kinds of skeleton.

activities.record: A table with two columns: hard part outside, and hard part inside. Write one gain and one cost in each column.
activities.context: In this activity a groundnut in the shell and a date are models of two kinds of skeleton. One has the hard part on the outside, like a crab. The other has it inside, like you.

setup.art: A groundnut in the shell and a date side by side on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Take one thing that is hard outside and one that is hard inside.

setup.art: A child pressing a groundnut shell between finger and thumb, and then pressing a date the same way.
setup.caption: 2. Press each one gently. Which soft part is protected?

setup.art: The groundnut shell split open with the seeds inside, and the date cut open to show the stone.
setup.caption: 3. Open both. Find the hard part and the soft part of each.

flow.do: Put the two things on a plate. Your child presses each one gently between finger and thumb, without breaking it.
flow.say: Press each one gently. In which one do your fingers meet the hard part first? In which one do they meet the soft part first?
flow.kid: Press each one gently. Where is the hard part? Where is the soft part?
flow.parent: These are parts of plants, used here only as models. The groundnut shell stands for an exoskeleton. The stone of the date stands for a bone.
flow.context: This is the first step of Shell or Stone. You press a hard-outside thing and a hard-inside thing.

flow.do: Open both. Ask the three questions below, one at a time.
flow.say: Suppose the soft part had to grow to twice the size. In which one would the hard part get in the way? In which one is the soft part open to a scratch?
flow.kid: Open both. Which soft part could grow bigger? Which could be scratched?

ask.q: The soft part inside a hard shell must grow. What has to happen to the shell?
good: The shell has to split.
A new, bigger shell is needed.

ask.q: Which plan protects the soft part better from a scratch?
good: The hard shell outside.

flow.context: In this step of Shell or Stone you open both things. You compare how the hard part protects and limits the soft part.

flow.do: Write one gain and one cost of each plan in the table. Then name two animals for each plan.
flow.say: A crab is built like the groundnut, with the hard part outside. You are built like the date. Name one gain and one cost of each plan.
flow.kid: Write one gain and one cost for each plan. Name two animals for each.

check.q: Why must a crab moult to grow, when a child does not?
options: A crab's hard coat cannot stretch
check.why: A hard coat on the outside sets the size of the body, so it has to be shed and replaced. Bones are inside the soft parts and grow along with them.

flow.context: This is the last step of Shell or Stone. You write down a gain and a cost of a hard part outside and of a hard part inside.

projects.title: Bone Builder Diary: three days of bone food, sunlight and jumps

materials.item: a notebook page for the diary
a pencil
a skipping rope, if you have one

schedule.what: Learn the three things bone cells need, draw the diary table and fill in today.
Fill in the diary and do the 50 jumps.
Fill in the diary, add up the three days and choose one thing to change.

projects.record: A table with three rows, one for each day, and three columns: calcium foods I ate, minutes in sunlight, and minutes of running, jumping or skipping.
projects.context: In this three-day project you keep a diary of the three things your bone cells need to build strong bone: calcium from food, sunlight on your skin, and the loading of running and jumping.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of three rows for Day 1, Day 2 and Day 3, and three columns headed Calcium foods, Sunlight minutes and Jumping minutes.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a diary table with three rows and three columns.

setup.art: A plate with a ragi dosa, a small bowl of curd and a spoonful of sesame chutney, with a girl skipping on a sunny terrace in the background.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, write your calcium foods, your minutes in the sun and your minutes of jumping.

setup.art: The diary table filled in, with totals at the bottom and one box circled.
setup.caption: 3. On day 3, add up each column. Circle the one you want to raise.

flow.do: Day 1. Read the list of calcium foods below with your child and tick the ones your family eats. Draw the diary table. Fill in today's row together. Then your child does 50 jumps or skips.
flow.say: Your bone cells need three things. They need calcium from food. They need vitamin D, which your skin makes in sunlight. And they need to feel your bones being loaded. Which of these did you get today?
flow.kid: Bones need calcium, sunlight and jumping. Draw the diary. Fill in today.
flow.parent: Foods rich in calcium: milk, curd, buttermilk, paneer, ragi, sesame seeds, drumstick leaves, amaranth leaves, rajma, chana, and small fish eaten whole. Ragi has many times more calcium than rice or wheat. About 15 minutes of sun on the arms and legs in the morning is a reasonable aim. Do not let skin burn.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Bone Builder Diary. You learn what bone cells need and start a three-day diary.

flow.do: Day 2. In the evening, fill in the second row. Your child does 50 jumps or skips and adds those minutes.
flow.say: What calcium foods did you eat today? How many minutes were you in the sun? How long did you run, jump or skip?
flow.kid: Fill in today's row. Do 50 jumps. Add the minutes.
flow.wait: Do this the day after you start the diary
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Bone Builder Diary. You fill in the diary for calcium foods, sunlight and jumping.

flow.do: Day 3. Fill in the third row. Add up each column for the three days. Your child chooses one column to raise next week and says how.
flow.say: Add up your three days. Which column is the smallest? Bone that you build now will still be with you when you are old. What one thing could you change?
flow.kid: Add up each column. Which is the smallest? What will you change?
flow.wait: Do this on the third day

ask.q: Why is jumping in the diary, when it is not a food?
good: Bone cells build more bone where the bone is loaded.
Astronauts lose bone when their legs carry no weight.

flow.parent: There is no score to reach. The aim is for your child to see that bone is built from food and sunlight, and shaped by use.
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Bone Builder Diary. You add up three days and choose one thing to change.

challenges.title: The Quick Hand: move a hand 15 centimetres with a 3 centimetre pull
challenges.problem: In the Ruler Arm experiment, a band tied close to the elbow end lifted the coins far. It needed only a short pull. Now build a cardboard arm with an elbow joint, flat on a table. The hand must move 15 centimetres when you pull the string only 3 centimetres.
constraints: The arm has two parts, an upper arm and a forearm, joined at an elbow that bends.
The forearm is 30 centimetres long and carries two coins taped at the hand end.
The arm lies flat on a table, and the upper arm is taped down.
You may pull the string no more than 3 centimetres.
The hand end must move at least 15 centimetres.
The string must not snap or tear the cardboard.
materials: two strips of thick cardboard from a carton, each about 30 centimetres long and 4 centimetres wide
a short piece of string or wire to tie the elbow joint
a long piece of strong string, about 60 centimetres
general: Tie the string to the forearm 6 centimetres from the elbow. A pull of 3 centimetres there moves the hand end about 15 centimetres.
Start with the forearm at a right angle to the upper arm, and pull the string along the upper arm.
Stick tape over the place where the string is tied, so the cardboard does not tear.
creative: Add a rubber band behind the elbow as a second muscle, so the arm straightens again when you let go.
Thread the string through a small paper loop on the upper arm. Then it runs close to the bone, as a real tendon does.
Tie the string even closer to the elbow. See how small a pull can still move the hand 15 centimetres.
challenges.your_turn: Now change your arm so that it can also throw. Put a small ball of paper on the hand. Find the tying place that sends the ball furthest across the table with one quick pull. Measure three throws and write the distances.
challenges.context: In this challenge you build a cardboard arm with an elbow. You must find where to tie the string so that a short pull moves the hand a long way.

setup.art: Two cardboard strips joined end to end by a loop of string through two holes, lying on a table in an L shape, with two coins taped to the free end of one strip.
setup.caption: 1. Join two cardboard strips with string at the elbow. Tape two coins on the hand end.

setup.art: The cardboard arm lying flat on a table in an L shape, the upper arm strip taped down, and a long string tied through a hole in the forearm strip a short way from the elbow and running along the upper arm strip.
setup.caption: 2. Tape the upper arm to the table. Tie a long string to the forearm and lay it along the upper arm.

setup.art: A child pulling the string a short distance marked 3 centimetres on a ruler, while the hand end of the cardboard forearm swings across the table.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the string 3 centimetres. Measure how far the hand moves.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look again at the results of the Ruler Arm experiment. Ask where the string should go.
flow.say: In the Ruler Arm experiment, which tying place moved the coins furthest for the shortest lift of the band? Where will you tie the string on this arm?
flow.kid: Read the problem. Where should the string be tied? Why?

ask.q: What is the cost of tying the string very close to the elbow?
good: The string must pull much harder.
The cardboard may tear.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Quick Hand. You plan where to tie the string, using the results of the Ruler Arm experiment.

flow.do: Make a hole near one end of each strip and tie them loosely together to make the elbow. Tape the coins on the far end of the forearm. Your child ties the long string to the forearm at the place they chose.
flow.say: Build the arm. The elbow must bend freely. Tie the string where you planned, and mark that place with the pencil.
flow.kid: Build the arm. Tie the string where you planned.
flow.parent: Make the holes yourself with the pencil point, on a folded towel. Leave the elbow knot a little loose so the joint turns.
flow.context: In this step of the Quick Hand you build the cardboard arm and tie the string muscle to the forearm.

flow.do: Lay the arm flat on the table in an L shape and tape the upper arm down. Lay the string along the upper arm. Mark the place of the hand end on the table. Mark 3 centimetres on the string. Your child pulls exactly that far. Measure how far the hand end has moved. Record it.
flow.say: Pull the string just 3 centimetres and hold. I will measure how far the hand has moved from its mark. Did it reach 15 centimetres?
flow.kid: Pull the string 3 centimetres. Measure how far the hand moves.
flow.context: In this step of the Quick Hand you test whether a 3 centimetre pull moves the hand 15 centimetres.

flow.do: If the hand moved less than 15 centimetres, move the string and test again. Then talk about the question below.
flow.say: Change one thing and test again. Which way did you move the string, and what happened to the pull you needed?
flow.kid: Move the string. Test again. What changed?

check.q: You move the string closer to the elbow of a model arm. What happens?
options: The hand moves further, with a harder pull
The hand moves less, with an easier pull
check.why: Close to the joint, a short pull turns the forearm through a big angle, so the hand travels far. But the pull has to be much stronger to hold the same load.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Quick Hand. You improve your cardboard arm and say what the change cost.

items.p: Which bones make a hard box round the brain?
items.why: The skull is a box of bones round the brain. The ribs guard the heart and lungs, and the pelvis guards the bladder and lower gut.

items.p: Which word means that a muscle gets shorter and pulls?
items.why: A muscle contracts when it shortens and pulls on a bone. It relaxes when it stops pulling.

items.p: The longest bone in the body is the thigh bone, also called the ____.
items.why: The femur runs from the hip to the knee. In a grown-up it is about a quarter of the person's height.

items.p: A muscle can push a bone as well as pull it.
items.why: False. A muscle works by getting shorter, so it can only pull. A second muscle on the opposite side pulls the bone back.

items.p: Match each part of the skeleton to what it protects.
items.why: Each of these bones lies round something soft. Press gently on each one on your own body, and think about what is behind it.

items.p: Sort these animals. Is the skeleton inside the body or outside it?
items.why: Birds, frogs and fish have a backbone and bones inside. Ants, crabs and spiders have a hard coat outside, with the muscles within.

items.p: A rubber band lifts a ruler arm that carries coins. Where must it be tied to stretch the most?
items.why: The ruler is a lever that turns at the pressed end. A pull close to that end must be much bigger to hold up the same coins. If you chose 'closest to the coins', that is where the pull is smallest.

items.p: Bone in a living body has blood vessels and living cells.
items.why: True. Living bone is pink and wet. Its cells build new bone and remove old bone all through life, and this is how a broken bone mends.

items.p: Put these in order, to show how you bend your elbow.
items: A nerve signal reaches the biceps
The tendon pulls on the forearm bone
The forearm turns at the elbow
a: A nerve signal reaches the biceps
The tendon pulls on the forearm bone
The forearm turns at the elbow
items.why: The muscle pulls only after a signal reaches it. The pull passes through the tendon to the bone, and the bone turns at the joint.

items.p: A strong cord that joins a muscle to a bone is called a ____.
items.why: Bend your arm and press into the bend of your elbow. The tight cord you feel is the tendon of your biceps.

items.p: Why must a young cockroach moult?
items.why: An exoskeleton is hard and fixed in size. To grow, the cockroach splits the old coat and grows a bigger one.

items.p: Explain in two sentences why your arm needs both a biceps and a triceps.
items.a: The biceps can only pull the forearm up, because a muscle cannot push. The triceps on the other side pulls the forearm back down to straighten the arm.
items.why: A strong answer says that muscles only pull, and that the two muscles pull in opposite directions.

items.p: Name two jobs of your skeleton and give one example of each.
items.a: Any two of these. Support: the leg bones and backbone hold me up. Protection: the skull guards the brain. Movement: muscles pull on the arm bones to throw a ball. Making blood: marrow in the bones makes blood cells.
items.why: A strong answer names two different jobs and gives a real bone or body part for each.

items.p: Label five bones on this skeleton: skull, ribs, backbone, pelvis and femur.
a: Skull: the bones of the head
Ribs: the curved bones round the chest
Backbone: the chain of small bones down the back
Pelvis: the ring of hip bones
Femur: the thigh bone, from hip to knee
items.why: A strong answer puts each label on the right bone. The femur is the single bone of the thigh, above the knee.
items.art: A front view of a human skeleton with five blank label lines pointing to the skull, the ribs, the backbone, the pelvis and one thigh bone.

items.p: Which of these foods is rich in calcium for building bone?
items.why: Ragi, milk, curd, sesame seeds and drumstick leaves are rich in calcium. Sugar, oil and salt have almost none.

items.p: The biceps joins the forearm close to the elbow. What does the body gain from this?
opts: The hand moves far and fast
items.why: A short pull close to the joint swings the hand a long way, quickly. The cost is that the muscle must pull much harder than the load weighs.

items.p: Which part of bone stops a crack from running straight through it?
items.why: Collagen fibres lie across the path of a crack and hold the two sides together. The mineral makes bone hard, but mineral alone would snap like chalk.

items.p: An astronaut floats in space for six months. What happens to her leg bones?
opts: They lose bone and get weaker
items.why: Bone cells build bone where it is loaded. In space the legs carry no weight, so bone is removed faster than it is built.

items.p: A tortoise can climb out of her shell.
items.why: False. The shell is made from her ribs and backbone, grown wide and joined together. It is part of her skeleton.

items.p: A shark's skeleton is made of cartilage, with no bone.
items.why: True. Cartilage is the firm, bendy material in your ear. A shark's whole skeleton is made of it.

items.p: Sort these facts. Is each one about an exoskeleton or an endoskeleton?
items: It must be shed for the animal to grow
It covers the outside of the body
It grows along with the body
The muscles are wrapped round it
It can hold up an elephant
items.why: An exoskeleton is a hard coat outside the muscles, so it protects the surface but must be shed. An endoskeleton is inside the muscles and grows with the body.

items.p: Three of these animals have an exoskeleton. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: A scorpion, a prawn and an ant each have a hard coat on the outside. A gecko has a backbone and bones inside.

items.p: A load weighs 2 kilograms. The arm muscle pulls 8 times as hard. How many kilograms of force is that?
items.why: 8 times 2 is 16. The muscle pulls with about 16 kilograms of force, because it is joined so close to the elbow.

items.p: Put these in order, to show how a child's long bone grows longer.
items: Cartilage cells in the growth plate divide
In the late teens the growth plate turns to bone
a: Cartilage cells in the growth plate divide
In the late teens the growth plate turns to bone
items.why: New cartilage is made first, and bone then replaces it from behind. When the whole plate has turned to bone, the bone can no longer grow in length.

items.p: A stick of chalk snaps, and a rubber band bends. Explain why a bone does neither.
items.a: Bone is made of two materials together. The hard mineral stops it bending like rubber. The collagen fibres stop it snapping like chalk. So bone is both hard and tough.
items.why: A strong answer names both materials and says what each one adds.

items.p: An arm spends six weeks in a plaster cast. Explain why it comes out thinner.
items.a: The arm was not used, so its muscles were not worked and its bone was not loaded. Unused muscle gets thinner, and bone cells remove bone that is not loaded.
items.why: A strong answer says that muscle and bone both change with use. Six weeks of rest is enough to see it.

items.p: A bat's wing and a whale's flipper contain the same bones. What does this tell scientists?
items.a: It tells them that bats and whales come from the same ancestors, who had a limb with those bones. Over a very long time the same bones changed shape for flying and for swimming.
items.why: A strong answer says the bones are shared because of shared ancestors, not because the jobs are alike.

items.p: Engineers are designing a robot to explore a rocky planet. They disagree about its body.

views.says: Give it a hard shell on the outside. A shell keeps out dust and protects the parts from knocks.
Give it a frame on the inside. Then we can make it large, and add new parts without rebuilding the shell.
Give it a soft body with no hard frame. It could squeeze into cracks that the others cannot enter.

items.ask: Which body would you choose? Give a reason from what you know about animal skeletons. Then say one cost of your choice.
items.a: Any choice with a reason from the unit. For example: a shell protects well, as a crab's does, but it limits size. A frame inside allows a large body, but the outside is unprotected. A soft body squeezes through gaps, but it is slow on land.
items.why: Each plan has real gains and costs, as in living animals. A strong answer gives a gain, names a cost and uses an animal as evidence.

items.p: Draw an insect's leg and your own arm, both cut open. Show where the muscles are in each.
items.a: The insect's leg is a hard tube with the muscles inside it. The arm has the bones in the middle with the muscles wrapped round them and skin on the outside.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the hard part outside the muscles in the insect, and inside the muscles in the arm.
items.art: A blank box divided in two, with the headings 'Insect leg' and 'My arm'.

items.p: A hard skeleton on the outside of an animal's body is called an ____.
items.why: 'Exo' means outside. A skeleton inside the body is called an endoskeleton.

items.p: A ruler arm's band is tied at 10 centimetres. The load is at 30 centimetres. How hard must the band pull?
items.why: The load is 3 times as far from the turning point as the band is. So the band must pull about 3 times as hard as the load pulls down.

items.p: A mole digs hard. A horse runs fast. In which animal is the arm muscle joined further from the joint?
items.why: A muscle joined further from the joint gives more force and less speed, which suits digging. A muscle joined close to the joint gives speed, which suits running.

items.p: Which test best shows that mineral is what makes bone stiff?
opts: Soak one bone in vinegar, one in water
Weigh a bone on a kitchen scale
Measure how long a bone is
items.why: Vinegar dissolves the mineral, and the bone goes bendy. The bone in water shows that soaking alone does not do this.

items.p: The oldest fish fossils with bone have bony plates in the skin and no bony backbone. What does this suggest?
opts: Bone began on the outside of the body
Bone was always inside the body
items.why: The first bone was a coat of plates in the skin. Bone inside the body, such as a bony backbone, came later.

items.p: Every grown-up human has exactly the same number of bones.
items.why: False. 206 is the usual count. Some people have an extra rib, or extra small bones in the hands and feet.

items.p: When you stand still, none of your muscles are working.
items.why: False. Muscles in your legs, back and neck pull gently all the time. Without them your skeleton would fold at the joints.

items.p: Match each animal to the surprising fact about the skeleton.
pairs: The shell is made from ribs and backbone
Tiny hard plates lie under the skin
The only hard part is a beak
items.why: Where the hard part lies does not always tell you the kind of skeleton. You have to ask what the hard part is made from and whether it is under the skin.

items.p: About one tenth of a grown-up's bone is replaced each year. How many years to replace a whole skeleton's worth?
items.why: Ten tenths make one whole. So in about 10 years, as much bone as a whole skeleton has been taken away and built again.

items.p: Body parts that come from the same part in a shared ancestor are called ____.
items.why: Your arm, a bat's wing and a whale's flipper are homologous. They have the same bones because of a shared ancestor.

items.p: A band lifting a ruler arm stretched most when tied near the pressed end. The load never changed. Explain why.
items.a: The ruler is a lever that turns at the pressed end. A pull close to the turning point has little turning effect. So it must be much bigger to hold up the same load. A bigger pull stretches the band more.
items.why: A strong answer says that the ruler turns about the pressed end. It also says that a pull close to that point has to be bigger.

items.p: Ice with paper in it survives a drop that breaks plain ice. Explain what the paper fibres do.
items.a: When a crack starts in the ice, the fibres lie across it and hold the two sides together. The crack cannot run straight through, so the slab stays in one piece.
items.why: A strong answer says that the fibres stop a crack from spreading. Collagen fibres do the same job in bone.

items.p: No land animal with an exoskeleton is as big as an elephant. Give one reason why.
items.a: A hard coat thick enough to hold up a huge body would be very heavy. Also, the animal is soft after each moult. A huge soft body on land would sag under its own weight.
items.why: A strong answer links size to the weight of the coat or to the danger of moulting. Either reason is accepted.

items.p: Many people think bones are dead, like stones. What evidence would you show them?
items.a: A broken bone mends. Children's bones grow longer. A tennis player's serving arm has thicker bone, and astronauts lose bone in space. Stones do none of these things.
items.why: A strong answer gives at least two things that living bone does and a stone does not.

items.p: Three people talk about the place where the arm muscle joins the forearm.

views.says: It should join further from the elbow. Then the same muscle could lift a much heavier weight.
Close to the elbow is right. A short pull whips my hand round fast, and speed is what I need.
No one place is best. A mole's digging arm is built for force, and a horse's leg is built for speed.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using what a ruler arm test shows. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that a band tied near the pressed end moved the load furthest for a short lift. Another is that a band tied further out needed less force.
items.why: Each speaker is right about something. A strong answer uses both sides of the lever: force is gained only by giving up distance and speed.

items.p: Draw your forearm as a lever. Mark the elbow, the place where the muscle pulls, and the load.
items.a: A bar turning at one end, marked 'elbow'. An arrow pulling up very close to that end, marked 'muscle'. A weight at the far end, marked 'load in the hand'.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the muscle's pull between the elbow and the load, and much closer to the elbow.
items.art: A blank box with a faint outline of a bent arm holding a ball.

quiz.p: About how many bones does a grown-up human have?
quiz.why: The usual count is 206. A baby has more separate pieces, and some join together during childhood.

quiz.p: Where are more than half of your bones?
quiz.why: Each hand has 27 bones and each foot has 26. That makes 106 of the 206.

quiz.p: What does the red marrow inside your bones make?
quiz.why: Red marrow makes about two million new blood cells every second. Making blood is one of the hidden jobs of the skeleton.

quiz.p: The backbone protects a thick bundle of nerves. What is the bundle called?
quiz.why: The spinal cord runs through holes in the vertebrae. It carries signals between the brain and the body.

quiz.p: Which two materials together make bone both hard and tough?
quiz.why: The mineral of calcium and phosphate makes bone hard. The collagen fibres make it tough, so that it does not snap.

quiz.p: Where does a child's long bone grow longer?
opts: At growth plates near its ends
In the middle of the bone
quiz.why: Growth plates are bands of cartilage near each end of a long bone. New cartilage is made there, and bone replaces it.

quiz.p: Your elbow is bent. Which muscle must contract to straighten it?
opts: The triceps, at the back of the arm
The biceps, at the front of the arm
quiz.why: The triceps pulls on the back of the forearm and straightens the elbow. The biceps bends it, and a muscle cannot push.

quiz.p: In a fair test of a ruler arm, what is the one thing you change?
opts: The place where the band is tied
The height the coins are lifted
quiz.why: The coins, the band and the lifting height stay the same. Then any change in the stretch of the band must come from the tying place.

quiz.p: A muscle is joined to a bone very close to the joint. What does that mean for its pull?
opts: It must pull much harder than the load
It pulls less hard than the load
It pulls exactly as hard as the load
It does not need to pull
quiz.why: A pull close to the turning point has to be bigger to hold up a load far away. Your arm muscles pull about 8 times harder than the load in your hand.

quiz.p: Which of these animals has an exoskeleton?
quiz.why: A prawn has a hard coat on the outside. A frog and a shark have a skeleton inside, and an earthworm has no hard skeleton.

quiz.p: What is one cost of having an exoskeleton?
opts: The animal is soft after each moult
The skeleton makes too much blood
quiz.why: A hard coat cannot stretch, so it must be shed. Until the new coat hardens, the animal is soft and easy to catch.

quiz.p: A human arm and a bat's wing have the same bones. Why?
opts: It is only a chance likeness
quiz.why: The ancestors of all four-limbed vertebrates had a limb with these bones. Over millions of years the same bones changed shape for different jobs.

applications: Doctors use the way bone mends itself. A plaster cast or a metal plate only holds the broken ends still, and the bone cells do the joining.
Surgeons replace worn hip and knee joints with metal and plastic ones. Sensors inside some of these joints showed how large the forces in the body are.
A digger arm on a building site is a lever like your forearm. The piston that moves it pushes close to the joint, so a short push swings the bucket a long way.
Bicycle frames, bamboo scaffolding and tent poles are hollow tubes, like long bones. A tube is stiff and light.
Builders put steel rods in concrete and glass fibres in plastic. The fibres or rods stop cracks from running through, as collagen does in bone.
Scientists who study old graves and crime scenes work out a person's height and age from the bones. Mildred Trotter's rules for height from the thigh bone are still used.
Engineers build suits with a powered frame on the outside for people who cannot walk. They call such a suit an exoskeleton, after the outside skeleton of an insect.
