open_questions.q: Why did animals first make bone?
open_questions.why_open: The oldest bone was armour in the skin of early fish. Scientists argue about whether it began as a shield, a store of minerals or part of a sense organ. Fossils alone may never settle it.

open_questions.q: How does a bone cell sense that the bone is being loaded?
open_questions.why_open: Bone cells sit in tiny spaces filled with liquid. When a bone bends a little, the liquid moves, and most scientists think the cells sense that movement. The steps from there to building new bone are still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Does the human skeleton send chemical messages that change how the body uses sugar?
open_questions.why_open: It seemed so in some mice. Other teams could not repeat the result, and studies in humans do not yet agree.

open_questions.q: What makes the pop when a knuckle is cracked?
open_questions.why_open: A gas bubble in the liquid of the joint is involved. A study with a scanner in 2015 said the pop comes as the bubble forms. A study with mathematics in 2018 said it comes as the bubble partly collapses.

open_questions.q: How can people keep their bones on a journey to Mars?
open_questions.why_open: The trip would take many months with no weight on the legs. Exercise machines slow the loss of bone but do not stop it fully. Nobody has yet tested a trip that long.

ask_kids: When you lift your school bag, which muscle is pulling? Can you feel it go hard?
Why do you think you crack a nut with your back teeth and not your front teeth?
If you had a hard coat like a crab, what would be easier? What would be harder?
Where on your body can you feel a tendon move?
Which calcium foods did we eat today?
A door opens easily at the handle. Why is it so hard to push near the hinges?
The cockroach we saw was white. What had just happened to her?
Which of your bones do you think carried the most weight today?

jokes.j: What is a muscle's favourite game?
jokes.a: Tug of war. It never has to push.

jokes.j: Why did the crab go shopping?
jokes.a: She had grown out of everything she owned.

jokes.j: Why was the biceps so tired?
jokes.a: It did eight times the work, and the hand got all the praise.

jokes.j: Why did the tortoise never move house?
jokes.a: She was too attached to it.

jokes.j: What did the tendon say to the muscle?
What do you call an earthworm's skeleton?
Why is the rib cage such a good friend?
What did the femur say to the kneecap?
jokes.a: You are always getting in front of me.

jokes.j: Why did the cockroach stay home after moulting?
jokes.a: She had nothing hard to wear.

maths.problem: In the Ruler Arm experiment the coin end rose 12 centimetres every time. With the band tied at 5 centimetres, the thread loop rose only 2 centimetres. How many times as far as the loop did the coins move?
maths.explain: The coins moved 12 centimetres and the loop moved 2 centimetres. 12 divided by 2 is 6. So a short lift near the elbow end became a movement 6 times as long at the hand end.
maths.context: In the Ruler Arm experiment a rubber band lifts a ruler that carries coins. The band is tied by a thread loop 5, 15 or 25 centimetres from the pressed end. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the two distances shows how much the lever multiplies a movement. That number tells you what the body gains from joining a muscle close to a joint.

maths.problem: In the Ruler Arm experiment the loop rose 2 centimetres when tied at 5 centimetres. It rose 6 at 15 centimetres and 10 at 25 centimetres. Find the pattern. How far would the loop rise if it were tied at 10 centimetres?
maths.explain: Each time the tying place moves 10 centimetres along, the loop rises 4 centimetres more. That is 2 centimetres more for every 5 centimetres along. From 5 to 10 is one step of 5, so 2 plus 2 is 4.
maths.context: In the Ruler Arm experiment a rubber band lifts a ruler that carries coins. You measure how high the thread loop rises. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: A pattern in the results lets you predict a tying place you never tested. You can then test it and see whether the pattern holds.

maths.problem: A grown-up's biceps joins the forearm 4 centimetres from the elbow. A bag in the hand is 32 centimetres from the elbow. How many times as hard as the bag's weight must the muscle pull? What is the pull if the bag weighs 2 kilograms?
maths.answer: 8 times as hard. For a 2 kilogram bag, about 16 kilograms of force.
maths.explain: 32 divided by 4 is 8. The bag is 8 times as far from the elbow as the muscle is. So the muscle pulls 8 times as hard. 8 times 2 is 16. The real pull is a little more, because the forearm has weight too.
maths.context: In the Ruler Arm experiment you found that a band tied close to the pressed end must pull much harder. Your own arm muscle is joined close to the elbow in the same way.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two distances from the elbow gives a number for a real arm. It matches what you felt in the rubber band.

maths.problem: A grown-up has 206 bones. Each hand has 27 bones and each foot has 26. How many bones are in the two hands and two feet together? Is that more than half of all the bones?
maths.answer: 106 bones. Yes, that is more than half.
maths.explain: Two hands have 27 plus 27, which is 54. Two feet have 26 plus 26, which is 52. 54 plus 52 is 106. Half of 206 is 103, and 106 is more than 103.
maths.context: In Bone Labels you stuck the names of twelve large bones on a real person. Most of the body's bones are small ones that you did not label.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the small bones shows where most of the skeleton's parts are. Hands and feet need many small bones because they make many small movements.

maths.problem: Here are four people's heights and thigh bones. For whom is the thigh bone exactly one quarter of the height? A thigh bone 44 centimetres long is found. About how tall was that person?
maths.answer: The child and the mother. The person with the 44 centimetre thigh bone was about 176 centimetres tall.
maths.explain: A quarter of 132 is 33, and a quarter of 160 is 40. So the child and the mother fit exactly. A quarter of 148 is 37, and a quarter of 168 is 42. So the other two are 1 centimetre away. 4 times 44 is 176.
maths.context: In Thigh Bone and Height you cut a string as long as a person is tall. You folded it in four and held it against their thigh bone. These are made-up measurements.
maths.why_maths: Checking the quarter rule against several people shows how well it works. Then the rule can be used the other way, to estimate a height from one bone.

maths.problem: In a Paper Ice Test, three plain slabs first broke at drops of 20, 20 and 40 centimetres. Three paper slabs were all still in one piece after 80 centimetres. One plain slab lasted until 40 centimetres. Does that spoil the result? Why were three slabs of each kind better than one?
maths.answer: No, it does not spoil the result. Three slabs show how much the results vary.
maths.explain: Even the best plain slab broke at 40 centimetres, which is half the height that every paper slab survived. So the two kinds do not overlap. With one slab of each kind, a single odd slab could have misled you.

chart.title: Made-up results: the drop that first broke each slab

maths.context: In the Paper Ice Test you drop a slab of plain ice and a slab of paper ice. These are made-up results for three slabs of each kind.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance whether two groups of results overlap. Repeating a test shows whether a difference is real or a fluke.

warmup.q: About how many bones does a grown-up have?
Name three jobs of your skeleton.
warmup.a: It holds you up, protects soft organs and helps you move. It also makes blood.

warmup.q: What does a muscle do when it contracts?

warmup.a: No. Muscles only pull, so they work in pairs.

warmup.q: What joins a muscle to a bone?
What two materials is bone made of?
warmup.a: Hard mineral and tough collagen fibres.
A hard skeleton on the outside of the body, as on a crab or an ant.

warmup.q: Why does an insect have to moult?
warmup.a: The hard coat cannot stretch, so it must be shed for the insect to grow.

warmup.q: Is your arm muscle joined near the elbow or near the wrist?
warmup.a: Near the elbow. So it pulls much harder than the load in your hand.

quiz: A muscle can push a bone as well as pull it.
A muscle works by getting shorter, so it can only pull.
Bone in a living body has blood vessels and living cells.
Living bone grows, mends itself and is rebuilt all through life.
More than half of your bones are in your hands and feet.
The hands and feet hold 106 of the 206 bones.
A crab's skeleton is inside her body.
A crab has an exoskeleton, a hard coat on the outside.
Your arm muscle pulls harder than the weight in your hand.
It is joined close to the elbow, so it pulls about 8 times as hard.
A tortoise can leave her shell.
The shell is made from her ribs and backbone.
An insect must shed the old coat to grow.
A hard coat cannot stretch, so the insect moults.
A shark has no skeleton.
A shark has a skeleton made of cartilage.
Bone gets stronger where it is loaded often.
Bone cells build more bone where the bone is bent and squeezed.
Bone is made of mineral only.
Bone is mineral with tough collagen fibres, which stop it from snapping.
odd: An ant, a crab and a scorpion have an exoskeleton, but a frog has bones inside.
The skull, a rib and the femur are bones, but the biceps is a muscle.
An earthworm, a jellyfish and a slug have no hard skeleton, but a gecko has bones.
Milk, ragi and sesame seeds are rich in calcium, but sugar has almost none.
The arm, the wing and the flipper have the same bones inside. A claw is a hard tube with no bones.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1600s many scholars thought that the bones of the body worked like a crowbar. With a crowbar, a small push lifts a heavy stone. So they supposed that muscles lift heavy loads with small forces. Giovanni Alfonso Borelli, an Italian teacher of mathematics, doubted this. He looked at where muscles join the bones in humans and other animals. He found that almost every muscle joins its bone very close to a joint. That is the short side of the lever. Then he did the sums that are used for levers. They showed that the muscles which bend the elbow must pull many times harder than the weight in the hand. He did the same sums for the legs and the back. In his old age Borelli was poor and taught mathematics in a school in Rome. Queen Christina of Sweden, who lived in Rome, agreed to pay for printing his book. He died on the last day of 1679. The book, On the Movement of Animals, came out in 1680 and 1681. Some of his numbers were too large, but later measurements showed that his main idea was right.
how_we_found_out.who: Giovanni Alfonso Borelli, a teacher of mathematics in Italy, with Queen Christina of Sweden, who paid for his book
how_we_found_out.when: Borelli worked on the book for many years and died in 1679. It was printed in Rome in 1680 and 1681.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the body's levers help the muscles, so that a small muscle force lifts a big load. Borelli showed with the mathematics of levers that it is the other way round. Muscles join the bones close to the joints, so they must pull much harder than the load weighs.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in the clothes of the 1600s at a desk, drawing a bent arm holding a round weight, with lines and letters marking the elbow, the muscle and the hand.

roots.context: In this unit you lifted a ruler arm with a rubber band. You also found your own tendon in the bend of your elbow. Here we ask what goes on inside you that you never feel, and where your bones come from.

deep_truth.truth: In the Ruler Arm experiment, the band tied nearest the pressed end stretched most, though the coins never changed. Your biceps joins your forearm close to the elbow, like that band. So to lift a 1 kilogram bag of rice, the muscle pulls with about 8 kilograms of force. The forces inside your body are much bigger than the weights you lift.
deep_truth.habit: We feel a weight in the hand and suppose that our muscles pull just that hard. We judge the work of the body by what reaches the outside. The lever sums show that muscles, tendons and joints carry loads many times bigger than anything we hold.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Ruler Arm experiment the band was longest when tied 5 centimetres from the pressed end. That end also pushed up hard against the finger. Borelli worked out the same thing for real arms in 1680. Sensors inside artificial hip joints measure more than twice the body's weight at every step.

three.who_am_i: You are stronger inside than you feel. Each time you lift a tumbler, your muscles, tendons and bones carry several times its weight. You notice none of it.
three.what_is_life: Your bone cells sense each load and build bone where it is needed. A living body keeps rebuilding even its hardest parts to fit the way it lives.
three.what_is_this_world: The calcium in your bones came from your food, and before that from soil and rock. Much limestone rock was made from the shells and skeletons of sea animals. Hard parts of living beings become rock, and rock becomes hard parts again.

roots.thread: Your arm has the same bones as a bat's wing and a whale's flipper. All three came from one ancestor. The calcium in those bones came from rock, and all calcium was first made inside stars. So one body plan and one material appear in many different beings. Many sages taught that the many come from one source. The science of skeletons shows two plain cases of this: shared ancestors and shared atoms.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu that the body divides what we eat into three parts. He speaks of rich foods such as oil and ghee. Their coarsest part becomes bone, he says. The middle part becomes marrow, and the finest part becomes speech.
teachings.link: Uddalaka's list is not what science found. The mineral in bone comes from calcium in food, not from oil. But his main point is the same as this unit's: bone is not given once and for all. It is made from what we eat, day after day.

teachings.source: Milindapanha (The Questions of King Milinda), Book 2, the chariot
teachings.teaching: The monk Nagasena asks King Milinda whether the axle is the chariot, or the wheels, or the pole. The king says no to each. 'Chariot' is a name for all the parts working together.
teachings.link: 'Arm' is a name of the same kind. No bone, muscle or tendon lifts a tumbler alone. In the Ruler Arm experiment the ruler, the band and the pressing finger each had a part. The lifting needed all three.

science.text: Every calcium atom in your bones was made inside a star long ago, before the Earth formed. The atoms reached you through rock, soil, plants and food.
Bone cells sense the tiny bending of a loaded bone and signal other cells to build or remove bone. Exactly how they sense it is still being worked out.

other_view.who: Giovanni Borelli, René Descartes and many scientists since
other_view.view: They describe a body as a machine of levers, ropes and hinges. On this view a bone cell that adds bone under load is following chemical rules. A pressure cooker's weight lifts in the same way when the steam is strong enough. Nothing more needs to be said about sensing or deciding.

practice.title: Feel the hidden pull
practice.say: Sit and rest one forearm on your lap, palm up. Press two fingers of the other hand into the bend of that elbow. Now lift the forearm slowly, as if your hand held a full tumbler. Feel the cord under your fingers go tight. Hold it there for three slow breaths. Lower the arm and feel the cord go soft. That pull is there every time you lift anything. What is it like to notice it?
practice.kid: Rest your arm on your lap. Press into the bend of your elbow. Lift your forearm slowly. Feel the cord go tight. Take three slow breaths. Lower your arm.

ask: In the Ruler Arm experiment the band pulled hardest where it moved least. Your muscles pull like that all day. Why do you think you never feel how hard they pull?
Your bone cells add bone where you load it. So who shapes your skeleton: you, your cells, or the way you live?
The calcium in your thigh bone was once in rock, and before that in a star. In what way is the bone yours?

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step, but not yet done at home. The Ruler Arm experiment (core) needs a 30 centimetre ruler, a thin rubber band, thread, five coins, tape and a bottle. The pressed end of the ruler tries to jump up when the band is tied at 5 centimetres, so the child must press firmly. A thick rubber band may stretch too little to show a difference. The step says to add five more coins or use a thinner band. The loop heights of about 10, 6 and 2 centimetres follow from the shape of the lever and should come out in every home. The Paper Ice Test needs a freezer, two plates of the same size and two newspaper pages. It takes two days, with about 13 minutes on the first day and 17 on the second. The plain slab usually cracks or breaks from 20 to 40 centimetres, and the paper slab usually stays in one piece. Ice strength varies with how cold the freezer is and how fast you work, so the step says to write down what really happens and gives a spoon test if nothing breaks. Do the drops on a bathroom or balcony floor and dry the floor afterwards. Put the wet paper in the dustbin. Bendy Bone is only for families who cook chicken, and it is not in the core. Thin wing bones go bendy in about five days. A thick leg bone can take more than a week. Thigh Bone and Height is rough, because the thigh bone is measured through clothes and muscle. A difference of three finger-widths is normal. Lift and Press needs a table too heavy to lift. Shell or Stone uses plant parts as models and says so. The Quick Hand works best flat on a smooth table, with the upper arm taped down. Bone Labels, both games, the diary and the worksheets need only paper and pencil. No part needs a garden, a pet or a wild animal. Facts to treat with care: the figure of about 8 times for the arm muscle uses round numbers, 4 and 32 centimetres, and leaves out the weight of the forearm. The count of 206 bones is the usual one and varies between people. The loss of about one hundredth of hip bone each month in space is an average, and astronauts differ. Borelli's own numbers were often too large, though his idea was right. The ideas about why bone first appeared are marked as debated. The Chandogya verse is given as a paraphrase, and the unit says plainly that its list is not what science found. The story's puppet has one finger string to keep the idea clear, and the story note says that real bommalattam arms are usually moved with rods. The three videos have no address yet.
